# Commol Documentation

> A high-performance compartment modelling library for mathematical modeling

Commol is a Python library, with a Rust engine, to build, simulate and calibrate compartment models. Models are built with ModelBuilder, simulated with Simulation and fitted with Calibrator. Examples use abstract names (bins A, B, C; parameters k1, k2).


# Getting started

# Commol

Commol builds, simulates and calibrates compartment models: amounts move between states (compartments) at rates you write as formulas. An amount can be a count, a mass or a concentration. You describe the process once, in Python, and choose the engine that runs it: difference equations, differential equations or a stochastic process of whole units. A Rust engine expands the model over your stratifications, compiles every rate to machine code, runs it, fits it to your data and measures how sure the fit is.

Before version 1.0

The API can change between minor versions (`0.2` → `0.3`). The [changelog](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/about/changelog/index.md) marks every change that breaks code as **Breaking**.

## How Commol works

```
flowchart LR
    A[ModelBuilder: the process] -->|build with a structure and an engine| B[Model]
    B --> C[Simulation]
    C -->|run, replicates| D[Results: read, plot, report]
    B --> E[Calibrator]
    E -->|run| F[CalibrationResult]
    F -->|apply_calibration_parameters| B
    E -->|uncertainty| G[ParameterSample]
    G --> H[Predictive, Scenarios]
    H --> D
```

1. **Build** the process once with `ModelBuilder`: bins, parameters, transitions, stratifications and accumulators. `build` joins it with a structure (the amount each bin starts with) and an engine, and checks the whole definition.
1. **Run** it with `Simulation`. The same process runs as difference equations, as differential equations or as a stochastic process of whole units; only the engine changes.
1. **Read** the results by output name, and draw or report them with their own methods (`results.plot`, `results.report`).
1. **Calibrate** the unknown values against observations with `Calibrator`, and write the result back into the model.
1. **Quantify** how sure the fit is: an uncertainty method gives a sample of the parameters, and its predictive gives bands and scores.
1. **Compare** runs: `Scenarios` runs a sample under other parameter values, and `plot_compared` draws several results on the same panels.

Every parallel step (the starts of a calibration, the replicates, the draws of a predictive) runs in Rust on the threads you choose.

## Quick example

One process, run by two engines:

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

process = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
)
structure = Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0})

steps = Simulation(process.build(structure, engine="DifferenceEquations")).run(num_steps=100)
flows = Simulation(process.build(structure, engine="DifferentialEquations")).run(num_steps=100)
print(round(steps["C"][-1]), round(flows["C"][-1]))  # the amount of C in each model
```

# Installation

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

Install Commol from PyPI, or build it from source to work on it.

## Quick path

```bash
pip install commol
```

The figures need matplotlib, the optional extra `commol[plot]`:

```bash
pip install 'commol[plot]'
```

| Requirement                      | Version                                              |
| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Python                           | 3.12 or later                                        |
| Platforms with ready-made wheels | Linux and macOS (x86_64 and arm64), Windows (x86_64) |

On other platforms, `pip` builds Commol from the source distribution, which needs a Rust toolchain.

## Check the installation

```python
import commol

print(commol.__version__)
print(commol.build_info())
```

`commol.__version__` is the version you installed. `commol.build_info()` gives it with the full commit of the source; save it with a result to name the code that made it.

| Installed from                               | `__version__`                               | `build_info().commit`                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| A wheel of a release on PyPI                 | The release, such as `0.9.0`                | The commit of the release              |
| The source distribution of a release         | The release                                 | `None`: the source has no git metadata |
| A git commit, or a clone (`maturin develop`) | `0.1.0+g<first 7 characters of the commit>` | The full commit                        |

A build that is not a release has the placeholder version `0.1.0` of the source, so its local version (`+g…`) is what names its commit. The metadata of the package (`pip show commol`) gives the placeholder alone.

## Build from source

To work on Commol, or to use unreleased code from `main`:

1. Install Rust: `curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh`.
1. Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), at the version of `required-version` in `py-commol/pyproject.toml`; another version of uv refuses to run in the project. A standalone uv moves to it with `uv self update <version>`.
1. Clone, install the dependencies, and build the extension:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MUNQU/commol.git
cd commol/py-commol
uv sync --extra dev --extra docs
source .venv/bin/activate    # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
maturin develop --release --features test-kind
pytest
```

| Step                                             | Why                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `uv sync --extra dev --extra docs`               | Creates `.venv` with the test, lint and documentation tools. It does not build Commol (`package = false` in `pyproject.toml`), and a later `uv sync` removes the install of Commol.                                  |
| `source .venv/bin/activate`                      | `maturin develop` installs into the active environment.                                                                                                                                                              |
| `maturin develop --release --features test-kind` | Compiles the Rust extension and installs Commol in editable mode. The `test-kind` feature adds the model kind that the tests need; a release never has it. Run it again after every Rust change and every `uv sync`. |

Paths with spaces

Maturin may fail when the project path contains spaces. Clone into a path without them.

See [Development Workflow](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/development/workflow/index.md) for branches, checks and pull requests.

# Quick Start

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

Build a model, run it, read and plot its results, run the same process with another engine, and fit it to data. Each step takes a few lines. This page assumes Commol is installed with its figures (`pip install 'commol[plot]'`, see [Installation](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/getting-started/installation/index.md)).

## Quick path

1. Write the process with `ModelBuilder`: bins, parameters and transitions.
1. Build it with a structure (`Aggregate`, the amount each bin starts with) and an engine.
1. Run it with `Simulation`, read a series by its output name, and draw it with `results.plot`.

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

process = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
)
structure = Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0})

model = process.build(structure, engine="DifferenceEquations")
simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

print(simulation.simulation_outputs)  # ['A', 'B', 'C']
print(results.positions[-1], round(results["C"][-1]))  # 100.0 and the amount of C
results.plot.series(output_file="quickstart.png")  # one panel per bin
```

`results` maps each output name to its values, one per position from step 0 to step 100; `results.positions` holds the positions. `results.plot.series` returns the matplotlib `Figure`, and saves it when you give `output_file`.

## What each call does

| Call                                              | What it does                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `ModelBuilder(name=..., version=...)`             | Starts a model definition. Every method returns the builder, so calls chain.                                                   |
| `.add_bin(id="A", name="State A")`                | Adds a compartment (a *bin*): a state that holds an amount, in the unit of the bin.                                            |
| `.add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)`              | Adds a named value for rate formulas. `value=None` leaves it for calibration.                                                  |
| `.add_transition(..., rate="k1 * A * B / total")` | Moves an amount from `source` to `target` along the axis. This rate names compartments, so it is the flow itself (*absolute*). |
| `.add_transition(..., rate="k2")`                 | This rate names no compartment, so it is *proportional*: the flow is `k2 × B`.                                                 |
| `Aggregate(bin_amounts=...)`                      | The *structure*: the amount each bin starts with.                                                                              |
| `.build(structure, engine=...)`                   | Joins the *process* (what you wrote) with the structure and an engine, checks the definition and returns a `Model`.            |
| `Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)`            | Runs the model in the Rust engine and returns its `SimulationResults`.                                                         |
| `results["B"]`, `results.positions`               | The values of one output, and the positions they were read at.                                                                 |
| `results.plot.series(...)`                        | Draws each series along the axis.                                                                                              |

See [Core Concepts](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/core-concepts/index.md) for bins, transitions and [what a rate means](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/core-concepts/#what-a-rate-means) in each engine.

## One process, several engines

The process is written once. The same builder and structure build a model of another engine: differential equations in continuous time, or a stochastic process of whole units. `plot_compared` draws the runs on the same panels:

```python
from commol.plotting import plot_compared

differential = Simulation(process.build(structure, engine="DifferentialEquations"))
stochastic = Simulation(process.build(structure, engine="StochasticEvents"))

continuous = differential.run(num_steps=100)
replicates = stochastic.replicates(50, seed=1).run(num_steps=100)

print(len(replicates))  # 50 runs of whole units, one seed each
plot_compared(
    {"difference": results, "differential": continuous, "stochastic": replicates},
    series=["B"],
    output_file="engines.png",
)
```

A difference model applies each flow once per step; a differential model integrates the flows; a stochastic engine moves whole units at random, so `replicates` holds one run per seed and the figure shows their mean and band. See [Running Simulations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/index.md) and [Stochastic Simulation](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/stochastic/index.md).

## Check units

Give every bin and parameter a unit, and the unit of one step, and Commol checks that each rate gives the bin unit per step unit:

```python
model_with_units = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Model with Units", version="1.0", bin_unit="item", step_unit="day")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3, unit="1/day")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1, unit="1/day")
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
    .build(structure, engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

model_with_units.check_unit_consistency()  # raises UnitConsistencyError on a mismatch
```

See [Unit checking](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/units-and-equations/#unit-checking).

## Calibrate unknown parameters

Set the unknown parameters to `None`, describe the observations and the unknowns in a `CalibrationProblem`, and let an optimizer find the values:

```python
from commol import (
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
)

observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=value)
    for step, value in [(10, 45.2), (20, 78.5), (30, 62.3), (40, 38.1)]
]

calibration_model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Calibration Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=None)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=None)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
    .build(structure, engine="DifferenceEquations")
)

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=42,
)

# A simulation of a model with a parameter at None can be calibrated, not run.
calibration = Simulation(calibration_model)
result = Calibrator(calibration, problem).run()
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in result.best_parameters.items()})

calibration_model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)
fitted = calibration.run(num_steps=60)  # the simulation follows its model
fitted.plot.series(series=["B"], observed_data=observed_data, output_file="fit.png")
```

| Object                                                | Role                                                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ObservedDataPoint`                                   | One observation: a position (`at`), an output and a value.                                                      |
| `CalibrationParameter`                                | One unknown, with its bounds.                                                                                   |
| `CalibrationProblem`                                  | The observations, the unknowns, the loss, the optimizer and the `seed` of its random numbers.                   |
| `Calibrator(...).run()`                               | Runs the optimizer in Rust and returns a `CalibrationResult` (`best_parameters`, `final_loss`, `converged`, …). |
| `Model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)` | Writes the calibrated values into the model.                                                                    |

See [Model Calibration](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/index.md) for initial conditions, constraints, scale factors and the optimizers.

## Log messages

Commol logs with the standard `logging` module, to the logger `commol` and its children: the root module logs as `commol`, and each other module as its name, such as `commol.resampling` or `commol.plotting`. Commol adds no handler of its own: your application chooses where the messages go. Python shows only warnings and errors until you configure logging.

To see the messages of commol and of every other library, configure the root logger once, at the start of your program:

```python
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

Simulation(model).run(num_steps=10)
```

Each message shows its level and its logger, such as `INFO:commol:Running simulation for 10 steps.`

| To                                                  | Call                                                                        |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| See the messages of every library                   | `logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)`                                   |
| Set a level for commol only                         | `logging.getLogger("commol").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)`                       |
| Send the messages of commol to a place of their own | `logging.getLogger("commol").addHandler(logging.FileHandler("commol.log"))` |
| Read the messages of one module only                | `logging.getLogger("commol.resampling")`, with a level or a handler         |

See the [logging HOWTO](https://docs.python.org/3/howto/logging.html) for handlers, formats and levels.

## Checklist

- [ ] The model builds without errors.
- [ ] `Simulation(model).run(...)` returns one series per output, and `results.plot.series()` draws them.
- [ ] Another engine runs the same process when you change only `engine`.
- [ ] `check_unit_consistency()` passes when you give units.
- [ ] Calibration returns `best_parameters` within the bounds you set.

# User guide

# Core Concepts

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

A Commol model is a set of **compartments** that each hold an **amount**, and **transitions** that move amounts between them along the **axis**, the independent variable of the model (time is the most common one). The amounts of every compartment together are the **state** of the model, and their sum is the **total**. An amount can be a count, a mass or a concentration. This page explains each building block once, with a runnable example. For every option of every method, see [Building Models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/building-models/index.md).

## The concepts at a glance

| Concept           | What it is                                                                                            | Builder method             |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| Compartment (bin) | A state that holds an amount                                                                          | `add_bin`                  |
| Stratification    | A dimension that splits every compartment into categories                                             | `add_stratification`       |
| Parameter         | A named constant or formula used in rates                                                             | `add_parameter`            |
| Transition        | A flow between compartments, with a rate                                                              | `add_transition`           |
| Accumulator       | A counter of what a transition moved; not part of the state                                           | `add_accumulator`          |
| Process           | The bins, stratifications, transitions and accumulators: what changes and how, written once           | the `add_*` methods        |
| Structure         | How the process is laid out; `Aggregate` holds amounts per compartment and says how much starts where | `Aggregate(...)`           |
| Model             | The validated definition: a header, a process, a structure and an engine                              | `build(structure, engine)` |
| Simulation        | Runs a model for a number of steps                                                                    | `Simulation(model).run`    |

## Compartments

A compartment (a *bin*) holds an amount, in the unit of the bin. A model can have any number of them, with any ids.

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation, StratificationCondition

builder = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Concepts")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
)
```

## Parameters

A parameter is a named value that rates can use. Its value is a number, a formula (a string that can use other parameters and the [special variables](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/mathematical-expressions/index.md)), or `None` when calibration will find it.

```python
builder = (
    builder
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3, description="A to B rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1, description="B to C rate")
)
```

## Transitions

A transition moves an amount from its `source` compartments to its `target` compartments along the axis. How much it moves depends on its rate:

| The rate…                          | Kind             | Flow            | Example                |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------------- | --------------- | ---------------------- |
| names a compartment or a bin total | **Absolute**     | the rate itself | `"k1 * A * B / total"` |
| names no compartment               | **Proportional** | rate × source   | `"k2"` moves `k2 × B`  |

```python
builder = (
    builder
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
)
```

The engine decides the kind when the model is built, and [`model.describe()`](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/describing-models/index.md) shows the result: the proportional rate above shows as `k2 * B`. [Transitions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/transitions/#absolute-and-proportional-rates) gives the exact rule, with its edge cases.

## Accumulators

An accumulator counts what a transition has moved since step 0. It is an output of the simulation, not part of the state: nothing is ever taken from it, and it is not part of the total.

```python
builder = builder.add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
builder = builder.add_transition(
    id="t_ab_counted",
    source=["A"],
    target=["B"],
    rate="0.01 * A",
    accumulators=["cum_ab"],
)
```

With stratifications, an accumulator expands like a bin (`cum_ab_g1`, `cum_ab_g2`, …). Resetting a simulation sets it back to 0.

## Initial conditions: the structure

The calls above write the **process**: what changes and how. The **structure** lays the process out. `Aggregate` holds an amount per compartment, and gives the amount that each bin starts with, in the unit of the bin. An amount is a real number, finite and not negative:

```python
structure = Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 900, "B": 100, "C": 0})
```

Every bin needs an amount. An amount may be `None` when calibration will find it ([Model Calibration](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/index.md)). [The structure](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/building-models/#the-structure-aggregate) lists every argument of `Aggregate` and when each rule is checked.

## Build and run

`build` joins the process with the structure and an engine, validates the definition and returns a `Model`. `Simulation` runs it in the Rust engine:

```python
model = builder.build(structure, engine="DifferenceEquations")

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=50)

print(sorted(results))   # ['A', 'B', 'C', 'cum_ab']
print(len(results["A"]))  # 51: step 0 to step 50
```

A `Model` has a header (its name, parameters and step unit), the `process` (bins, stratifications, transitions and accumulators), the `structure` that lays it out, and the `engine` that runs it. The process is written once; the structure is what changes between kinds of model, so `ModelBuilder` builds every kind its process fits. Here `model.structure` is an `Aggregate`:

```python
print(model.engine.type)                    # DifferenceEquations
print(model.structure.kind)                 # aggregate
print([b.id for b in model.process.bins])   # ['A', 'B', 'C']
print(model.structure.bin_amounts)          # {'A': 900.0, 'B': 100.0, 'C': 0.0}
```

Four engines run an aggregate model, with the same process and structure:

| Engine                  | Time                                                                    | Crate                 |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `DifferenceEquations`   | Advances in whole steps; each step applies every flow once.             | `commol-difference`   |
| `DifferentialEquations` | Continuous: the engine integrates `dX/dt = Σ flows` with an ODE solver. | `commol-differential` |
| `StochasticEvents`      | Continuous, at random: whole units move one event at a time.            | `commol-stochastic`   |
| `StochasticSteps`       | Whole steps, at random: each step draws how many units each flow moves. | `commol-stochastic`   |

See [Differential equations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#differential-equations) and [Stochastic Simulation](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/stochastic/index.md).

### What a rate means

A flow is per unit of the axis in every engine, and the unit check is the same for every engine. What its value means is the engine's (`rate_meaning` of the engine's list, `EngineType` in `crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs`):

| Engine                  | `rate_meaning` | A flow of value `f`                                                                                              | Equation                               |
| ----------------------- | -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `DifferenceEquations`   | `per_step`     | Moves `f` in one step: the flow of an absolute rate, or `f × source` for a proportional rate                     | `X(n+1) = X(n) + Σ flows`              |
| `DifferentialEquations` | `continuous`   | Is the instantaneous rate of change: over a short span `Δ` it moves about `f × Δ`                                | `dX/dt = Σ flows`                      |
| `StochasticEvents`      | `continuous`   | Is the propensity of its events: the expected number of units it moves per unit of the axis                      | `dX/dt = Σ flows`, in the mean         |
| `StochasticSteps`       | `per_step`     | Is the expected number of units it moves in one step; a proportional rate is the probability that one unit moves | `X(n+1) = X(n) + Σ flows`, in the mean |

So one rate gives two different dynamics: a proportional rate `k` keeps `(1 - k)^n` of its source after `n` steps in a difference model, and `exp(-k n)` in a differential model. To find the rate that gives a mean span or a probability over a period in the engine of a model, use [`AxisUnits`](#units-of-the-axis): it asks the engine.

## Stratifications

A stratification splits every compartment into one compartment per category. The expanded name is `{bin}_{category}`, with one suffix per stratification, in the order the stratifications are declared:

```text
Bins: A, B           Stratification group = [g1, g2]

A -> A_g1, A_g2
B -> B_g1, B_g2      4 compartments (2 bins x 2 categories)
```

With several stratifications, the expansion is the product of all their categories:

```text
Stratifications group = [g1, g2] and type = [t1, t2]

A -> A_g1_t1, A_g1_t2, A_g2_t1, A_g2_t2      8 compartments for 2 bins
```

The initial amount of each compartment is the amount of its bin times the product of the fractions of its categories:

```python
stratified = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stratified")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9000, "B": 1000},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4}},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

for compartment in stratified.structure.initial_state(stratified.process):
    print(compartment.name, compartment.amount)
```

| Compartment | Calculation | Initial amount |
| ----------- | ----------- | -------------- |
| `A_g1`      | 9000 × 0.6  | 5400           |
| `A_g2`      | 9000 × 0.4  | 3600           |
| `B_g1`      | 1000 × 0.6  | 600            |
| `B_g2`      | 1000 × 0.4  | 400            |

`model.structure.initial_state(model.process)` returns this table as the engine builds it: each compartment with its bin, its categories and its amount.

Use a stratification when subgroups have different rates, when you need output per subgroup, or when the data you fit is broken down by category.

### Conditional stratifications

A stratification with `conditions` only splits the compartments whose earlier categories satisfy all of them. A condition may only name a stratification declared before it.

```text
Stratifications group = [g1, g2] and subtype = [s1, s2] (only where group = g2)

A -> A_g1, A_g2_s1, A_g2_s2      3 compartments per bin instead of 4
```

```python
conditional = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Conditional")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(
        id="subtype",
        categories=["s1", "s2"],
        conditions=[StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="g2")],
    )
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9000, "B": 1000},
            stratification_fractions={
                "group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4},
                "subtype": {"s1": 0.5, "s2": 0.5},
            },
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

print([c.name for c in conditional.structure.initial_state(conditional.process)])
# ['A_g1', 'A_g2_s1', 'A_g2_s2', 'B_g1', 'B_g2_s1', 'B_g2_s2']
```

The fractions of a conditional stratification are fractions of the subgroup it splits, not of the whole bin, so they multiply along the chain. `subgroup_total` sums the initial state over the compartments of a subgroup, and `get_conditioning_categories` names the subgroup:

```python
aggregate, process = conditional.structure, conditional.process
print(aggregate.subgroup_total(process))                 # 10000
print(aggregate.subgroup_total(process, ["g2"]))         # 10000 x 0.4 = 4000
print(aggregate.subgroup_total(process, ["g2", "s1"]))   # 4000 x 0.5 = 2000
print(aggregate.get_conditioning_categories(process, "subtype"))  # ('g2',)
```

See [Conditional Stratifications](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/building-models/#stratifications) for the full API.

### Per-compartment overrides

When the product of fractions cannot express the starting state, for example a state that is empty in only one category, `compartment_amounts` overrides single expanded compartments. Each amount is in the unit of the bin of its compartment and replaces the product for that compartment only:

```python
overridden = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Override")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9000, "B": 1000},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.5, "g2": 0.5}},
            compartment_amounts={"B_g1": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

print({c.name: c.amount for c in overridden.structure.initial_state(overridden.process)})
# B_g1 starts empty; the other compartments keep their product
```

| Rule                                   | Checked when       |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------ |
| Each amount is finite and not negative | `Aggregate(...)`   |
| Each name is an expanded compartment   | The model is built |

An override may hold more than the product gave its compartment: the bins keep no sum. `model.structure.update_compartment_amounts(model.process, {"B_g1": 50})` changes or adds overrides on a built model; the engine checks them against the expansion of the process before they are stored.

### Updating the initial state after building

```python
overridden.structure.update_bin_amounts({"A": 8500, "B": 1500})
overridden.structure.update_stratification_fractions({"g1": 0.7})  # g2 becomes 0.3
```

| Method                            | Rule                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `update_bin_amounts`              | Each amount is finite and not negative, or `None` for calibration. The other bins keep their amounts.                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `update_stratification_fractions` | Within each stratification you may omit one category; it receives what remains of 1, or 0 when the given fractions pass 1. Omitting two raises. Each fraction is from 0 to 1 and the fractions sum to 1 within 1e-6, with the rule of the engine; a rejected call changes no fraction. |

A category name that two stratifications declare must be qualified with its stratification, as in `{"group:g1": 0.5}`. Calibration writes its results back through these same methods.

## Several sources or targets

A transition can have several sources or several targets. It then moves **one** flow, which each source loses and each target gains, so its rate must be absolute. For independent flows of one formula from several compartments, the `$compartment` placeholder makes one transition per compartment. See [Several sources or targets](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/transitions/#several-sources-or-targets).

## Units of the axis

A model knows only steps: a rate is per step, and a position or a period is a number of steps. `AxisUnits` converts values in units to steps, and gives the rate that the engine of a model reads. `Model.axis_units()` gives the one of a model: its `step_unit` (or `step` when it declares none), its `origin` and its engine.

```python
from commol import AxisUnits

hourly = AxisUnits(step_unit="hour")

print(hourly.steps(1, "day"))     # 24.0
print(hourly.steps(3, "day"))     # 72.0
print(hourly.steps(30, "minute")) # 0.5

along_a_line = AxisUnits(step_unit="meter")
print(along_a_line.steps(2, "km"))  # 2000.0
```

`steps` works for any dimension, and raises `ValueError` for a unit of another dimension than the step, naming both units. It returns a `float`: whether a position must be a whole number of steps is the engine's check, made where the position is used. A result within `1e-9` of an integer is that integer.

The rate conversions ask the engine what a rate means ([What a rate means](#what-a-rate-means)):

| Method                                             | `DifferenceEquations` (`per_step`)                         | `DifferentialEquations` (`continuous`) |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `rate_from_mean_span(span, unit, keep="survival")` | `1 - exp(-1 / n)`, with `span` equal to `n` steps          | `1 / n`                                |
| `rate_from_mean_span(span, unit, keep="mean")`     | `1 / n`, with `span` equal to `n` steps and `n >= 1`       | `1 / n`                                |
| `rate_from_probability(p, period, unit)`           | `1 - (1 - p) ** (1 / n)`, with `period` equal to `n` steps | `-ln(1 - p) / n`                       |

```python
difference = AxisUnits(step_unit="day", engine="DifferenceEquations")
differential = AxisUnits(step_unit="day", engine="DifferentialEquations")

print(difference.rate_from_mean_span(4, "day", keep="survival"))  # 0.2212
print(difference.rate_from_mean_span(4, "day", keep="mean"))      # 0.25
print(differential.rate_from_mean_span(4, "day", keep="survival"))  # 0.25
print(difference.rate_from_probability(0.3, 1, "week"))
print(differential.rate_from_probability(0.3, 1, "week"))
```

With either engine, a rate from a probability moves `p` of its bin over the period.

A per-step rate cannot keep both the survival and the mean of a residence, so `rate_from_mean_span` has a required argument `keep`, with no default: which one a model keeps is a modelling choice.

| `keep`       | Per-step rate     | What the bin does                                                                                                                                      | Use it when                                                          |
| ------------ | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"survival"` | `1 - exp(-1 / n)` | Keeps `exp(-k / n)` at each step `k`, as the continuous process does; its mean residence is `1 / rate` steps (`4.52` for a span of 4, `10.508` for 10) | The step discretizes a continuous process                            |
| `"mean"`     | `1 / n`           | Keeps `(1 - 1/n)^k` at each step `k`: a geometric residence whose mean is `n` steps                                                                    | The step is the unit of the process, such as a cycle or a generation |

A continuous rate is `1 / n` with both values. With `keep="mean"`, a per-step rate needs a span of at least one step: a shorter one raises `ValueError`, which names the span in steps. Another value of `keep` raises `ValueError` with both values.

An axis of time with an origin also converts between dates and positions, and gives the ends of calendar days and weeks; see [Dates on the axis](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/units-and-equations/#dates-on-the-axis).

The axis also gives the window grid. A window has a width, a span in a unit, which must be a whole number of steps; any other width raises `ValueError`, naming the span, its unit and the step unit. A width in steps is the span in the step unit, such as `(7, "day")` for 7 steps of a day, or `(7, "step")` when the model declares no step unit.

| Method                                                     | Returns                                                                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `window_start(i, span, unit)`, `window_end(i, span, unit)` | The positions that bound window `i`: `i · width` and `(i + 1) · width`, with the width in steps                                           |
| `window_index(at, span, unit)`                             | The window that holds a position, `max(ceil(at / width) − 1, 0)`; the inverse of `window_end`. Reports place observations with this rule. |
| `window_ends(span, unit, end)`                             | Every complete window end up to the position `end`                                                                                        |

```python
print(hourly.window_start(0, 1, "week"), hourly.window_end(0, 1, "week"))  # 0.0 168.0
print(hourly.window_end(2, 1, "week"))       # 504.0
print(hourly.window_index(168, 1, "week"))   # 0
print(hourly.window_index(168.5, 1, "week")) # 1
print(hourly.window_ends(1, "day", 100))     # [24.0, 48.0, 72.0, 96.0]
```

A window covers the positions `(start, end]`, the same interval that [windowed observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/#counts-per-period-windows) use. [Windowed totals](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#windowed-totals) reads the gain of a series over each window.
