# Model Calibration

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

Calibration finds the parameter values (and, if you want, initial conditions and observation scale factors) that make a model reproduce observed data. You describe the observations and the unknowns in a `CalibrationProblem`, and a `Calibrator` runs an optimizer in the Rust engine.

| Topic                                                              | Page                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The workflow, the problem, losses and results                      | This page                                                                                                             |
| Maximum likelihood with a model of the noise of each series        | [Observation Models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md)             |
| Calibrating initial conditions                                     | [Calibrating Initial Conditions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-initial-conditions/index.md) |
| Several outputs, aggregates, weights, scale factors, windowed data | [Observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/index.md)                         |
| Nelder-Mead and particle swarm settings                            | [Optimizers](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/index.md)                             |
| Relations the result must respect                                  | [Constraints](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-constraints/index.md)                           |
| Reports of a calibrated model and run                              | [Reports](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/reports/index.md)                                               |
| Samples, predictive bands and scores                               | [Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/index.md)                                       |

## Quick path

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def basic_model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None, engine="DifferenceEquations"):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            ),
            engine=engine,
        )
    )

# Observations generated from k1 = 0.4, k2 = 0.1
truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step])
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

# 1. A model whose unknowns are None
model = basic_model(None, None)

# 2. The problem: observations, unknowns, loss and optimizer
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=42,
)

# 3. Calibrate
result = Calibrator(Simulation(model), problem).run()
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in sorted(result.best_parameters.items())})
# {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}

# 4. Write the values back, and simulate
model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)
calibrated = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)
```

A `Simulation` follows its model: after `apply_calibration_parameters` or `update_parameters`, its next `run` (and its `engine`) uses the new values, also when it was created while a parameter was `None`. See [Simulations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#simulation).

## The problem

| `CalibrationProblem` field    | Type                                                                 | Default  | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `observed_data`               | `list[ObservedDataPoint]`                                            | required | What the model must reproduce. See [Observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `parameters`                  | `list[CalibrationParameter]`                                         | required | The unknowns and their bounds.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `loss_function`               | `str \| None`                                                        | `None`   | How the misfit is measured; see [Losses](#losses). A problem has `loss_function` or `observation_models`, exactly one.                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `observation_models`          | `dict[str, NormalObservations \| … \| BinomialObservations] \| None` | `None`   | One observation model per series label: the fit maximizes their likelihood. See [Observation Models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md).                                                                                                                                      |
| `optimization_config`         | `NelderMeadConfig` or `ParticleSwarmConfig`                          | required | The optimizer and its settings. See [Optimizers](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `constraints`                 | `list[CalibrationConstraint]`                                        | `[]`     | Relations the result must respect. See [Constraints](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-constraints/index.md).                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `normalize_observations`      | `bool`                                                               | `False`  | Divides each residual by the RMS of its observation series, so series of very different size weigh the same. Needs a loss.                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `initial_condition_remainder` | `str \| None`                                                        | `None`   | The compartment or bin that absorbs the difference when initial conditions are calibrated. See [Calibrating Initial Conditions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-initial-conditions/index.md).                                                                                                           |
| `replicates`                  | `int \| None`                                                        | `None`   | How many replicates of a stochastic engine each evaluation runs. Required with a stochastic engine. See [Stochastic engines](#stochastic-engines) and [Stochastic Simulation](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/stochastic/index.md).                                                                                 |
| `replicate_summary`           | `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"crps"`, `Quantile(q)` or `None`              | `None`   | What each observation is compared with when an evaluation runs replicates. Required with a stochastic engine. See [Stochastic engines](#stochastic-engines).                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `seed`                        | `int \| None`                                                        | `None`   | The seed of every random number of a calibration: the replicates of a stochastic engine, the starts, a particle swarm and the uncertainty methods. Without it, the engine draws one, which `Calibrator.seed` gives. See [Reproducibility](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#reproducibility). |

### Observations

An `ObservedDataPoint(at=..., output=..., value=...)` is one observed value of an output at a position on the axis. Its other fields observe a sum of outputs, weigh it, scale the prediction by a factor or compare a gain over a window: [Observations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-observations/index.md) lists them all.

### Unknowns

| `CalibrationParameter` field | Type            | Default  | Meaning                                                           |
| ---------------------------- | --------------- | -------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `id`                         | `str`           | required | What to calibrate; depends on `parameter_type`.                   |
| `parameter_type`             | `str`           | required | `"parameter"`, `"initial_condition"`, `"factor"` or `"noise"`.    |
| `min_bound`, `max_bound`     | `float`         | required | The search interval.                                              |
| `initial_guess`              | `float \| None` | `None`   | Where the optimizer starts; the midpoint of the bounds if `None`. |

| `parameter_type`      | `id` names                                                                                                                                      | The value is                                                                                                                                                                            |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"parameter"`         | A model parameter with a number, or one declared with `value=None`; not a formula or a series parameter, which the engine computes at each step | The parameter value                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `"initial_condition"` | A bin, a category, or an expanded compartment                                                                                                   | An amount in the unit of its bin, or the split of a category; see [Calibrating Initial Conditions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-initial-conditions/index.md) |
| `"factor"`            | Any new id, used by observations through `factor_id`                                                                                            | A factor on the predictions; not part of the model                                                                                                                                      |
| `"noise"`             | Any new id, named by an [observation model](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/#noise-parameters)       | An argument of the model, such as its standard deviation; not part of the model                                                                                                         |

`"parameter"`, `"factor"` and `"noise"` work with every kind of model. The other types are values of the model kind, and the kind declares which it accepts (`model.structure.calibration_value_types()`): an aggregate model accepts `"initial_condition"`. A type the kind does not accept raises a `ValueError` that names the kind when you create the `Calibrator`. A `"parameter"` that the model does not have, or that a formula or a series sets, raises a `ValueError` with the engine's message at the same time.

## Losses

A problem has a loss or observation models, exactly one, and neither has a default: what to fit is a modelling choice. A loss measures the residuals; [observation models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md) say how each series scatters, and the fit maximizes their likelihood, so its loss is `−log L`. `CalibrationProblem` raises a `ValueError` with both or neither.

| `loss_function` | Formula (residual `r = observed − predicted`, weight `w`) | Use when                              |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `"sse"`         | `Σ w·r²`                                                  | The usual choice                      |
| `"rmse"`        | `√(Σ w·r² / Σ w)`                                         | You want the error in the data's unit |
| `"mae"`         | \`Σ w·                                                    | r                                     |

How weights count

Every loss uses a weight the same way: `weight=2.0` makes an observation count twice as much as one with weight 1.0. With every weight at its default of 1.0, the losses are the plain sum of squares, root mean square and mean absolute error. `LossConfig` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/types.rs` computes them; the discrepancy (`crates/commol-calibration/src/discrepancy.rs`) applies them.

With `normalize_observations=True`, each residual is first divided by the RMS of the observations of its series (its `label`).

A run the model does not allow gets a penalty instead of a loss: a run with values that are not finite, or a difference step that leaves an amount below zero (`InfeasibleStateError`, see [Amounts below zero](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/transitions/#amounts-below-zero)). The penalty is much larger than any fit, and the run is not recorded in the history, so the optimizer moves away from it and goes on. Any other error of a run, such as a rate that cannot be evaluated or that is not a number, stops the calibration with its message (`OptimizationObjective` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/objective.rs`, the only place that turns an infeasible point into a penalty).

## Stochastic engines

With a stochastic engine, one run per evaluation would make the loss change from one evaluation to the next for the same parameters, and Nelder-Mead and particle swarm would chase the noise. So each evaluation runs `replicates` replicates with **common random numbers**: the same replicate seeds at every evaluation, derived from `seed`. The loss is then a deterministic function of the parameters (`CalibrationProblem::with_replicates` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs`).

You choose what each observation is compared with; there is no default, because what to fit is a modelling choice:

| `replicate_summary` | Compared with each observation               | Loss                                         |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `"mean"`            | The mean of the replicates                   | `loss_function`                              |
| `"median"`          | The median                                   | `loss_function`                              |
| `Quantile(q)`       | The quantile `q`, a level between 0 and 1    | `loss_function`                              |
| `"crps"`            | The empirical distribution of the replicates | The continuous ranked probability score, \`E |

```python
stochastic = basic_model(None, 0.1, engine="StochasticSteps")
runs = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=runs["B"][step])
        for step in range(5, 51, 5)
    ],
    parameters=[CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=200),
    replicates=50,
    replicate_summary="crps",  # or "mean", "median", Quantile(0.9)
    seed=7,
)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(stochastic), problem).run()
print(round(result.best_parameters["k1"], 1))  # 0.4
```

| Rule                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | Where                                                                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A stochastic engine needs `replicates`, `replicate_summary` and `seed`; without one, `Calibrator` raises a `ValueError` that names the engine, and the message lists the summaries                                     | `CalibrationProblem::with_replicate_settings` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs`; `SimulationEngine::is_stochastic` |
| A deterministic engine does not use `replicates` and `replicate_summary`                                                                                                                                               | The same                                                                                                                                   |
| A stochastic engine needs a loss: with `observation_models`, `Calibrator` raises a `ValueError`                                                                                                                        | `CalibrationProblem::new`; `Discrepancy::set_summary`                                                                                      |
| The summaries and the CRPS are computed in `LossConfig`, and the observation weights apply to every option                                                                                                             | `LossConfig::replicate_loss` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/types.rs`                                                                   |
| The median and `Quantile(q)` are the one quantile of commol, the one of `weighted_quantiles` and `SimulationReplicates.quantiles` (NumPy's `method="hazen"`): `Quantile(0.25)` of the replicates 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is 1.75 | `ReplicateSummary::summarize`; `statistics::quantiles` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/statistics.rs`                                    |
| A constraint at positions is checked on every replicate                                                                                                                                                                | `CalibrationProblem::evaluate`                                                                                                             |

With one replicate the CRPS is the absolute error. The [predictive](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#the-predictive) of a sample runs every replicate of each draw.

## Results

`Calibrator(simulation, problem)` checks the problem against the model, and `run()` returns a `CalibrationResult`:

| `CalibrationResult` field | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `best_parameters`         | `dict[str, float]`: the best value of every unknown, in the order of `problem.parameters`                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `final_loss`              | The loss at `best_parameters`; with observation models, the negative log-likelihood                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `iterations`              | The optimizer iterations performed                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `converged`               | `True` only when the optimizer met its convergence test (a stop rule for a particle swarm); a run that used all `max_iterations` is `False`. See [Optimizers](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#converged-and-termination_reason). |
| `termination_reason`      | Why it stopped                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `starts`, `failed`        | Every start that finished, and each start that failed with its reason. See [Several starts](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#several-starts).                                                                                     |
| `seed`                    | The seed of the calibration's random numbers (`Calibrator.seed`). See [Reproducibility](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#reproducibility).                                                                                        |

```python
print(result.converged, result.termination_reason)
print(f"loss = {result.final_loss:.3g} after {result.iterations} iterations")
```

| `Calibrator` member                                     | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `run(starts=1)`                                         | Runs the optimizer from `starts` start points and returns the best `CalibrationResult`. See [Several starts](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#several-starts). |
| `run_with_history()`                                    | Returns a `CalibrationHistory`: the result and every evaluation of a feasible point.                                                                                                              |
| `uncertainty(method)`                                   | Runs an uncertainty method. See [Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#the-entry-point).                                                                          |
| `identifiability(method)`                               | Runs an identifiability method. See [Identifiability](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/identifiability/index.md).                                                          |
| `seed`                                                  | The seed of the calibration's random numbers: `problem.seed`, or a seed drawn once and logged.                                                                                                    |
| `num_observations`, `num_parameters`, `parameter_names` | Facts about the problem.                                                                                                                                                                          |

## Writing the result back

`Model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)` writes every calibrated value into the model, routed by its `parameter_type`:

| `parameter_type`      | Written to                                                                           |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `"parameter"`         | The model parameter with that id                                                     |
| `"initial_condition"` | The initial conditions, so the model rebuilds exactly the state the optimizer scored |
| `"factor"`, `"noise"` | Nothing: they describe the observations, not the model                               |

It accepts a `CalibrationResult` or a plain `{id: value}` mapping, such as one of `sample.draws()`; a `ParameterSample` has no single set of values and raises `TypeError`. It computes the new definition first, so a rejected value leaves the model unchanged. To set values by hand, use `Model.update_parameters({...})`.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every unknown is `None` in the model and has a `CalibrationParameter`.
- [ ] Every observation names an output of the model (`Simulation.simulation_outputs`).
- [ ] The bounds are realistic, and the result is not stuck at a bound.
- [ ] `result.converged` is `True`, or you know why not.
- [ ] You simulate the calibrated model (`apply_calibration_parameters`, then `run`).

# Calibrating Initial Conditions

[Back to Model Calibration](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/index.md)

An `initial_condition` unknown fits how the state starts: the amount of a bin in its unit, the split of a category, or the amount of one expanded compartment. The Rust engine applies the values in a fixed order, and a **remainder** compartment keeps the sum of the amounts the model states.

## Quick path

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def model_with_b(b_amount: float | None):
    # A holds what B does not, so A and B keep 1000 between them.
    a_amount = 1000 if b_amount is None else 1000 - b_amount
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Initial B")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": a_amount, "B": b_amount, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )

truth = Simulation(model_with_b(20)).run(num_steps=40)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step])
    for step in range(5, 41, 5)
]

model = model_with_b(None)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(
            id="B", parameter_type="initial_condition", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=100.0
        )
    ],
    initial_condition_remainder="A",
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=1000),
)

result = Calibrator(Simulation(model), problem).run()
print(round(result.best_parameters["B"], 2))  # 20.0

model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)
print({c.name: round(c.amount, 1) for c in model.structure.initial_state(model.process)})
# {'A': 980.0, 'B': 20.0, 'C': 0.0}
```

Here `B` is calibrated, and `A`, the remainder, takes what `B` leaves of the 1000 that the model states for `A` and `B`.

## What an id can name

| `id`                                      | Example                | The value is                                                                                                                               |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A bin                                     | `"B"`                  | The amount of the bin, in its unit. Its compartments share it in the proportions of the initial state, also when the `Simulation` has run. |
| A bin prefix (a bin and some categories)  | `"B_g1"`               | The amount in those compartments, shared in the same way. Compartments are matched by label, so `B_g1` never covers a bin `B_g1x`.         |
| An expanded compartment                   | `"B_g1_t2"`            | The amount of that compartment alone, in the unit of its bin.                                                                              |
| A category of a **binary** stratification | `"g1"` or `"group:g1"` | The split: every `(g1, g2)` pair of compartments keeps its total and gives `g1` this fraction.                                             |

A category that two stratifications share is written with its stratification, as in `"group:g1"` ([the same rule](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/core-concepts/#updating-the-initial-state-after-building) as for the initial state); a bare name is rejected as ambiguous.

The engine resolves every id when you create the `Calibrator` (`InitialConditionPlan` in `crates/commol-model/src/initial_conditions.rs`), so a wrong id fails before the optimization starts:

| `id`                                                                                                   | Error                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Names nothing in the model                                                                             | `Invalid bin, compartment or category 'X'`, with the compartments     |
| A category of a stratification with three or more categories, such as `"g1"` of `group = [g1, g2, g3]` | `Initial condition category 'group:g1' needs a binary stratification` |
| A category name that two stratifications declare                                                       | `… is ambiguous`, with the qualified names                            |

## The remainder

Without help, calibrated values change the sum of the amounts. Name a compartment or bin in `initial_condition_remainder`, and it takes what the values leave of the amounts the model states:

| Rule                                             | Detail                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| It is not calibrated                             | It takes the sum of the amounts the model states, less every other compartment.                                                                                                                                |
| It keeps the sum of what the values and it cover | A compartment that no value covers keeps its amount, so it does not change the remainder. A bin left `None` for calibration counts as 0, so the remainder states the sum: `A` holds 1000 while `B` is unknown. |
| It has the unit of every amount it gives         | The `Calibrator` rejects a calibrated bin, prefix or compartment whose unit is not the unit of the remainder, and names both. A category split has no unit.                                                    |
| It keeps its own split                           | A bin remainder shares what it takes across its compartments in the proportions of the initial state.                                                                                                          |
| It must not overlap a calibrated id              | Building the problem rejects it otherwise.                                                                                                                                                                     |
| A value that would make it negative is penalized | The optimizer moves away from it.                                                                                                                                                                              |

Without a remainder, values are applied as given, and the other compartments keep their amounts. So a model of a count in `A` and `B` and of a concentration in `C` can fit the amount of `C` alone, or fit `B` with `A` as the remainder.

## Order of application

Whatever their order in `parameters`, values are written in layers, like a model definition:

1. bins and bin prefixes;
1. category splits;
1. expanded compartments;
1. the remainder.

Within a layer, the order of `parameters` applies. So an expanded compartment always wins over the bin that contains it.

## One expanded compartment

Fitting a single compartment of a stratified model, such as a state that is empty in one group only, needs the remainder:

```python
def stratified(b_g1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Composite")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ba", source=["B"], target=["A"], rate="k1")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 900, "B": 100},
                stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.5, "g2": 0.5}},
                compartment_amounts={}
                if b_g1 is None
                else {"B_g1": b_g1, "A_g1": 500 - b_g1},
            ),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )

truth = Simulation(stratified(10)).run(num_steps=20)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="A_g1", value=truth["A_g1"][step])
        for step in range(2, 21, 2)
    ],
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(
            id="B_g1",
            parameter_type="initial_condition",
            min_bound=0.0,
            max_bound=100.0,
            initial_guess=30.0,  # Nelder-Mead is local: start near the answer
        )
    ],
    initial_condition_remainder="A_g1",
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=1000),
)

composite = stratified(None)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(composite), problem).run()
print(round(result.best_parameters["B_g1"], 2))  # 10.0

composite.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)
print({c.name: round(c.amount, 1) for c in composite.structure.initial_state(composite.process)})
# {'A_g1': 490.0, 'A_g2': 450.0, 'B_g1': 10.0, 'B_g2': 50.0}
```

## Writing back

`apply_calibration_parameters` writes the values so that the model rebuilds the state the optimizer scored:

1. Each bin whose every compartment a value or the remainder sets gets the amount the engine gave it, in the unit of the bin, and each category gets the split the engine applied, so the definition stays readable.
1. Every compartment whose amount still differs from the scored one is pinned as a `compartment_amounts` override.

So an expanded-compartment id always becomes an override, and so does a bin or category value that overlaps an existing override. A bin of which a value sets only some compartments keeps its amount. Reloading the saved model gives the scored state exactly. A calibrated category split is written with `update_stratification_fractions`: the named category gets the value and its complement the rest.

## Checklist

- [ ] Each unknown amount is `None` in the model, and the bounds are amounts in the unit of its bin (a category split is in `[0, 1]`).
- [ ] A remainder is named when the calibrated values should keep a sum, and it holds that sum in the model.
- [ ] The remainder has the unit of every amount it gives.
- [ ] The remainder is not also calibrated.
- [ ] Category ids name a binary stratification, qualified when the name is shared.

# Observations

[Back to Model Calibration](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/index.md)

An `ObservedDataPoint` says what the model must reproduce: an output at a position on the axis. This page shows how to observe several outputs, sums of outputs, partial observations (factors and known scales), counts per period (windows) and positions between integers, and how to weigh them.

## Quick path

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Observed")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
        .add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
        .add_transition(
            id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total", accumulators=["cum_ab"]
        )
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            ),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )

truth = Simulation(model(0.4)).run(num_steps=70)

def calibrate_k1(observed_data, **problem_options) -> float:
    problem = CalibrationProblem(
        observed_data=observed_data,
        parameters=[
            CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)
        ],
        loss_function="sse",
        optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
        **problem_options,
    )
    result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(None)), problem).run()
    return round(result.best_parameters["k1"], 3)

# Observe B and C at the same steps
observed = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output=output, value=truth[output][step])
    for step in range(10, 51, 10)
    for output in ("B", "C")
]
print(calibrate_k1(observed))  # 0.4
```

Each observation compares the model output named in `output` with `value` at the position `at`. Any output works: a compartment (`B`, `B_g1`) or an accumulator (`cum_ab`). The observation's `label` names its series in reports, plots and the per-series normalization; it defaults to `output`.

| Field       | Type                | Default  | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------- | ------------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `at`        | `float`             | required | The position on the axis. The engine decides which positions its model type accepts.                                                                                                                                      |
| `output`    | `str \| None`       | `None`   | The observed output. Give `output` or `outputs`, not both.                                                                                                                                                                |
| `outputs`   | `list[str] \| None` | `None`   | Outputs summed before the comparison; needs a `label`.                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `label`     | `str`               | `output` | The name of the observed series.                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `value`     | `float`             | required | The observed value, zero or more.                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `weight`    | `float`             | `1.0`    | Above zero. How much the observation counts in every loss, and the power of its term of a likelihood; see [Losses](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/#losses).                                      |
| `factor_id` | `str \| None`       | `None`   | A `factor` unknown that multiplies the prediction.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `scale`     | `float`             | `1.0`    | Above zero and finite. A known number that multiplies the prediction, with the factor; see [Known shares: scales](#known-shares-scales).                                                                                  |
| `window`    | `float \| None`     | `None`   | Compares with the gain over `(at − window, at]` instead of the value.                                                                                                                                                     |
| `trials`    | `int \| None`       | `None`   | The trials of the observation, for a `BinomialObservations()` model that reads them from each observation. See [Observation Models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md). |

An unknown field, such as a misspelt name, raises `ValidationError` and names it.

## Sums of outputs

When one measurement covers several outputs, list them in `outputs`. They are summed before the comparison; `label` names the sum for plots and reports:

```python
b_and_c = [
    ObservedDataPoint(
        at=step,
        label="B_plus_C",
        outputs=["B", "C"],
        value=truth["B"][step] + truth["C"][step],
    )
    for step in range(10, 51, 10)
]
print(calibrate_k1(b_and_c))  # 0.4
```

`outputs` may name compartments and accumulators, and works with `factor_id` and `window`. It must not be empty.

## Weights and normalization

| Option                        | Where                | Effect                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `weight=2.0`                  | `ObservedDataPoint`  | The observation counts twice as much, in every loss and in a [likelihood](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/#the-likelihood) ([How weights count](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/#losses)). |
| `normalize_observations=True` | `CalibrationProblem` | Divides each residual by the RMS of its series ([Losses](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration/#losses)), so a series of thousands does not drown a series of tens.                                                                         |

```python
weighted = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=10, output="B", value=truth["B"][10], weight=2.0),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=30, output="B", value=truth["B"][30], weight=1.0),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=30, output="cum_ab", value=truth["cum_ab"][30], weight=1.0),
]
print(calibrate_k1(weighted, normalize_observations=True))  # 0.4
```

## Partial observations: factors

When the data sees only part of an output, for example a fixed share of it, a `factor` unknown multiplies the prediction before the comparison. Link observations to it with `factor_id`:

```python
seen = 0.3
partial = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=seen * truth["B"][step], factor_id="share_seen")
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=partial,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="share_seen", parameter_type="factor", min_bound=0.01, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
)
scaled_result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(0.4)), problem).run()
print(round(scaled_result.best_parameters["share_seen"], 3))  # 0.3
```

| Fact                  | Detail                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Several factors       | Each observation names its own `factor_id`, so outputs can have different shares.                                                                                                                                      |
| Not part of the model | `apply_calibration_parameters` skips `factor` values.                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Plots                 | Pass `calibration_result=` to `results.plot.series` or `results.plot.observations`; it applies the calibrated factors to the comparison.                                                                               |
| Identifiability       | A rate and a share can explain the same data. Fit them together only when the data can tell them apart: [Identifiability](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/identifiability/index.md) checks it. |

## Known shares: scales

When the share an observation sees is known, give it as `scale`. The prediction is the sum of its outputs, or their gain over its window, times `scale` and times its factor, if it has one. The scale is a number, not an unknown: no method fits it, samples it or judges its identifiability, and it can change from one observation to the next.

```python
known = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=0.3 * truth["B"][step], scale=0.3)
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]
print(calibrate_k1(known))  # 0.4
```

| Fact         | Detail                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Counts       | A count model reads the mean `scale · model`, so the observed counts stay whole and keep their own size: a negative binomial of the counts seen on 1 unit in 40 reads `0.025 · model`, not the counts multiplied by 40. See [Observation Models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/#choosing-a-model). |
| Every reader | The loss, the likelihood, the predictive (`at_observations`), the scores, the resampling and conformal methods, the figures and the reports read an observation with its scale.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Figures      | `plot.series` and `plot.observations` draw the model times the scale; `plot.cumulative` divides each observed value by its scale and its factor.                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Reports      | The `observed` block of a report gives `scales` when a scale is not 1.0 ([Reports](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/reports/index.md)).                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| Range        | A scale of 0, below 0, infinite or NaN raises `ValidationError` that names `scale`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

## Counts per period: windows

Data often counts what happened **in** each period, such as the amount that entered a bin in each interval of 7 steps. Observe a cumulative output (an accumulator) with `window`, and the model's prediction becomes the gain over the window:

```text
predicted(at) = output(at) - output(at - window)
```

```python
ends = model(0.4).axis_units().window_ends(7, "step", 70)
counts = truth.windowed_totals(["cum_ab"], 7, ends)

windowed = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=end, output="cum_ab", value=count, window=7)
    for end, count in zip(ends, counts)
]
print(calibrate_k1(windowed))  # 0.4
```

| Rule                            | Detail                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The window starts at 0 or later | `at − window`, read as 0 within the rounding of the window; otherwise the observation is rejected when it is created, with the rule of the engine (`check_window_end` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/observation.rs`). |
| Any output                      | Usually an accumulator, but any compartment works.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Mixed windows                   | Observations may use different windows, and positions need not be multiples of the window.                                                                                                                                |
| Combinations                    | Works with `factor_id` and `outputs`.                                                                                                                                                                                     |

`SimulationResults.windowed_totals` applies the same reduction outside calibration, so a report shows exactly what the loss compared. See [Windowed totals](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#windowed-totals). An observation without `window` reads its output at `at`; `SimulationResults.sample` reads a run there in the same way ([Values at positions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#values-at-positions)).

## Positions between integers

An observation is at a position that the engine of the model reports at, as for [`Simulation.run_at`](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#simulation): a model in continuous time (`DifferentialEquations`, `StochasticEvents`) at any position, such as `2.5`, with windows of any length; a model of whole steps (`DifferenceEquations`, `StochasticSteps`) at integer steps only. The calibration reads the engine at those positions (`SimulationEngine::run_at_positions_into_buffer`), and the engine checks each one (`SimulationEngine::check_position`): `Calibrator` raises `ValueError` for a position the engine does not accept, and the engine's message names the observation, or the constraint, that holds it (`check_positions` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs`).

```python
def ode_model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Observed in continuous time")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0},
            ),
            engine="DifferentialEquations",
        )
    )

positions = [0.5, 1.75, 3.25, 6.5]
observed_b = Simulation(ode_model(0.2)).run_at(positions)["B"]
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=at, output="B", value=value)
        for at, value in zip(positions, observed_b)
    ],
    parameters=[CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
)
print(round(Calibrator(Simulation(ode_model(None)), problem).run().best_parameters["k1"], 3))  # 0.2
```

## Stratified models

Observe expanded outputs by name, such as `B_g1`, or sum them with `outputs`. `Simulation.outputs_for("B")` lists the names.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every `output` (and every entry of `outputs`) is an output name; a sum has a `label`.
- [ ] Weights say how much each observation counts, in every loss.
- [ ] Every `factor_id` has a `CalibrationParameter` with `parameter_type="factor"`.
- [ ] A known share is a `scale`, not a `factor` with narrow bounds.
- [ ] Windowed observations use a cumulative output and a window that starts at 0 or later.

| To learn                     | Read                                                                                      |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
