# Local Approximations: Laplace, Sandwich and Importance Sampling

[Back to Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/index.md)

These methods give fast uncertainty around a fit from the curvature of the objective there, with a few runs per parameter instead of one fit per replicate. The **Laplace approximation** is a normal centred on the fit; the **delta method** gives the band of the outputs from it with no run per draw; the **sandwich** holds when the noise model is wrong or the noise is dependent, and needs no noise model; the **Laplace mixture** puts a Laplace approximation at each optimum of a multi-start fit and corrects it towards the posterior by importance sampling, with a check of when that fails. They run in Rust (`crates/commol-inference/src/local/`) through `Calibrator.uncertainty`.

## Quick path

```python
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)
from commol.local import Laplace, LaplaceMixture, LikelihoodTarget, Sandwich
from commol.observations import NormalObservations
from commol.distributions import Priors


def flow_model(rate: str):
    """A flow from A to B each step, of the rate `rate`."""
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Flow")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_parameter(id="c", value=None)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate=rate)
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# The flow of each of 30 steps, 10 plus a normal noise of sd 1.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
flows = 10.0 + rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 30)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=float(value), window=1)
        for step, value in enumerate(flows, start=1)
    ],
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="c", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=30.0)
    ],
    observation_models={"B": NormalObservations(sd=1.0)},
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=3,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(flow_model("c * A / A")), problem)

laplace = calibrator.uncertainty(Laplace(draws=2000))
lower, upper = laplace.sample.interval(0.9)["c"]
print(round(lower, 2), round(upper, 2))  # 9.64 10.25

band = laplace.delta_band(calibrator, [10, 20, 30], 0.9)
print([round(value, 1) for value in band.center["B"]])  # [99.3, 198.7, 298.0]

sandwich = calibrator.uncertainty(Sandwich(block_length=1, draws=2000))
print(sandwich.blocks)  # 30
# The noise of these data is smaller than sd = 1: the sandwich reads it.
print(round(sandwich.covariance[0][0] / laplace.covariance[0][0], 2))  # 0.71
```

## The curvature and the unbounded scale

Every method of this page reads the curvature `H` of the objective at the fit: `−log L` of the [observation models](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/index.md), or the loss. The setting `curvature` of each method chooses it:

| `curvature`                | What it is                                                                                                                                                                     | Runs                          | Use it when                                                                 |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"gauss_newton"` (default) | The expected curvature: `Jᵀ W J`, with `J` the derivatives of the predictions and `W` the Fisher information of each observation, plus the information of each noise parameter | `4p + 1` (finite differences) | The model fits and the noise model is right or close                        |
| `"hessian"`                | The observed curvature: central differences of the objective                                                                                                                   | `4p² + 1`                     | The residuals are large, the mean is wrong, or the fit sits on a constraint |

The Fisher information of each observation model (`Noise::information` in `crates/commol-calibration/src/likelihood/density.rs`):

| Model                          | Mean `μ`                     | Noise arguments                                                       |
| ------------------------------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NormalObservations`           | `1/σ²`                       | `sd`: `2/σ²`                                                          |
| `LogNormalObservations`        | `1/(μ²σ²)`                   | `sigma`: `2/σ²`; with `center="mean"` also `1` and `−1/(μσ)` with `μ` |
| `StudentTObservations`         | `(ν+1)/((ν+3)s²)`            | `df` and `scale`, and their cross term                                |
| `PoissonObservations`          | `1/μ`                        |                                                                       |
| `NegativeBinomialObservations` | `1/(μ + φμ²)`                | `overdispersion`: the variance of its score, summed over the counts   |
| `BinomialObservations`         | `1/(n p (1 − p))`, `p = μ/n` |                                                                       |

The Hessian steps are `δ^{1/4} · dθ/du` for a parameter with a bound and `δ^{1/4} · max(|θ|, 1)` for one without, where `δ` is the accuracy of the engine (machine precision, or the `rtol` of the ODE engine): the step that balances the truncation error of the differences with the error of the runs, and keeps every run inside the bounds. Each entry of either curvature has an estimated error. An entry whose error is above 1 % of `√(H_jj · H_kk)` is listed in `notes` and logged as a warning. The error is read as a share of a correlation: an off-diagonal entry near 0 is compared with the diagonal of its row and column, not with its own size. A note changes no result.

Every distribution lives on the **unbounded scale** of the parameters, the scale on which the [sampler](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/smc/#how-the-sampler-works) of sequential Monte Carlo proposes its moves. The curvature there is `H_u = D · H · D` with `D = dθ/du` at the fit, and `covariance` is on that scale. Every draw maps back inside the bounds, so a fit near a bound gives a skewed sample, not draws outside it. A fit **on** a bound of its parameter (within `1e-8` of the width of its bounds, or of `max(1, |bound|)` when the parameter has one finite bound) raises a `ValueError`: its variance on the unbounded scale is infinite there, and a [profile likelihood](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/profiles/index.md) describes it.

## Laplace approximation and the delta method

`Laplace(draws, curvature="gauss_newton", starts=1)` fits the problem (`Calibrator.run(starts)`) and returns a `LaplaceResult`: the fit, the covariance `Σ = H⁻¹` of the normal on the unbounded scale, the draws mapped back (`sample`, equal weights) and the notes. It needs `observation_models`. A loss has no scale of the noise, and its curvature is no inverse variance, and `Laplace` with a loss raises a `ValueError`. To get a Laplace approximation, give a model with a noise parameter, such as `NormalObservations(sd="sd")` with `sd` calibrated, or use `Sandwich`, which needs none.

Every local approximation sits at the best of its `starts`, as [several starts](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#several-starts) of `Calibrator.run`. `Sandwich` takes `starts` the same way.

With a noise parameter the fit estimates the noise by maximum likelihood: for `NormalObservations(sd="sd")`, `σ̂² = SSE/n`, not `SSE/(n − p)`. The Laplace intervals are then narrower than the classical ones by `√(n/(n − p))`, which is negligible when `n ≫ p`.

`result.delta_band(calibrator, positions, confidence_level)` gives the band of every output by the delta method: the prediction at the fit plus and minus the quantile of the normal times `√(J Σ Jᵀ)`, with `J` the derivatives of the output on the unbounded scale. It runs the model a few times per parameter, not once per draw, and for a model linear in its parameters it equals the band of the draws (`Predictive(calibrator, result.sample, positions).band(confidence_level)`). It reads only the fields of the result, so a result read back from JSON works.

```python
widths = [round(high - low, 2) for low, high in zip(band.lower["B"], band.upper["B"])]
print(widths)  # [6.01, 12.01, 18.02]
```

## Sandwich

`Sandwich(block_length, draws, curvature="gauss_newton", starts=1)` gives the covariance `H⁻¹ B H⁻¹`, where `B` sums the outer products of the **scores** of blocks of observations: `B = G/(G − 1) · Σ_b s_b s_bᵀ`, with `s_b` the sum of the gradients of the terms of block `b` (the clustered estimator CR1, Cameron and Miller 2015). The blocks hold every series in a window of `block_length` positions, as the [bootstraps](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/resampling/#blocks-and-their-length) do; `"auto"` chooses the length of Politis and White (2004) from the residuals of the fit. It returns a `SandwichResult`: a `LaplaceResult` with `blocks` (`G`), `block_length` and the estimates of `"auto"`.

What the sandwich protects against depends on `H`:

| `curvature`      | It holds when                                                                                                       |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"gauss_newton"` | The noise model is wrong (its size changes, it is not normal, it is dependent inside a block) but the mean is right |
| `"hessian"`      | Also when the mean is wrong: the fit estimates the parameters that minimize the expected objective                  |

It needs no noise model: with a loss, `H` and the scores are those of the loss (the sum of squares and the root mean squared error share them, since rescaling the objective does not change the sandwich).

- **A Student t with `G − 1` degrees of freedom.** With few blocks, `B` is a noisy estimate; the t widens the intervals by the right amount, instead of a warning at an arbitrary number of blocks. Intervals of the draws and `LocalResult.delta_band` both read it.
- **`G ≤ p` is refused.** `B` sums `G` outer products whose sum has rank at most `G − 1` after the fit, so with no more blocks than parameters some directions would get zero variance. The `ValueError` suggests shorter blocks.
- **`loss_function="mae"` is refused.** The absolute error has no curvature: its sandwich would need the density of the residuals at 0, with a bandwidth that the library would choose for you. Use a [bootstrap](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/resampling/index.md).

## Laplace mixture and importance sampling

A multi-start fit can end at several optima. `LaplaceMixture(draws, target, curvature="gauss_newton", starts=1)` runs `Calibrator.run(starts)`, keeps the distinct ends (an end closer than one Mahalanobis unit to a kept one merges into it), puts a Laplace approximation at each, weights each by its Laplace evidence, draws from the mixture, and weights every draw by the target over the mixture on the unbounded scale. The largest weights are smoothed by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS, Vehtari et al. 2024).

| `target`                   | Density                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `LikelihoodTarget(priors)` | `prior(θ) · L(θ)`: the posterior of the observation models                                                                                      |
| `GibbsTarget(priors, eta)` | `prior(θ) · exp(−η · loss(θ))`: the [Gibbs posterior](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/smc/#gibbs-posterior) of the loss |

```python
# A flow c² has the two optima ±√ȳ.
square = problem.model_copy(
    update={
        "parameters": [
            CalibrationParameter(
                id="c", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=-5.0, max_bound=5.0,
                initial_guess=1.0,
            )
        ],
        "observed_data": [
            ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=float(value), window=1)
            for step, value in enumerate(4.0 + rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 10), start=1)
        ],
    }
)
mixture = Calibrator(Simulation(flow_model("c * c * A / A")), square).uncertainty(
    LaplaceMixture(
        starts=8, draws=2000, target=LikelihoodTarget(priors=Priors.uniform_on_bounds())
    )
)
print([round(component.center["c"], 2) for component in mixture.components])  # [2.05, -2.05]
print(round(mixture.k_hat, 2), mixture.reliable)  # 0.24 True
```

It returns an `ImportanceResult`: the fit, the weighted `sample`, the `components` (centre, weight, covariance, log evidence), `k_hat`, the `effective_size` and `reliable`.

### Reading `k_hat`

`k_hat` is the estimated shape of the tail of the importance weights: how far the mixture misses the target.

| `k_hat`    | Meaning                                                                                                                                                         |
| ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Up to 0.5  | The weights have a finite variance: the estimates converge at the usual rate                                                                                    |
| 0.5 to 0.7 | They converge, more slowly: use more draws                                                                                                                      |
| Above 0.7  | The mixture misses mass of the target, as for a curved (banana) posterior: `reliable` is false, `notes` and a warning say so, and the sample should not be used |

A start that ends on a bound gives no component, and `notes` says so. When its objective is at least as good as that of the worst kept component, the mixture leaves out an optimum the data support, whose mass `k_hat` cannot see: `reliable` is false too. An end on a bound that fits worse than every component only adds the note.

An unreliable sample calls for a method that samples the posterior itself: `BayesianPosterior` or `GibbsPosterior` ([Sequential Monte Carlo](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/smc/index.md)).

## When a local approximation is good enough

| Situation                                                                    | Good enough?                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A model near linear in its parameters around the fit, a correct noise model  | Laplace, with `LocalResult.delta_band` for the outputs                                                                                                                                                                                |
| A wrong or unknown noise model, dependent residuals, a right mean            | Sandwich with `"gauss_newton"` and blocks longer than the dependence                                                                                                                                                                  |
| A mean that may be wrong, large residuals                                    | Sandwich with `"hessian"`                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Several optima of equal or similar loss                                      | Laplace mixture; check `k_hat`                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| A curved posterior, a parameter whose data barely bound it, a fit on a bound | No: sample the posterior ([Sequential Monte Carlo](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/smc/index.md)), or a bootstrap ([Resampling](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/resampling/index.md)) |

## Checklist

- [ ] The fit is a minimum inside the bounds; no `ValueError` names a parameter on its bound.
- [ ] `notes` is empty, or you know why an entry of the curvature is uncertain.
- [ ] A Laplace approximation has a noise model you trust; otherwise use the sandwich.
- [ ] A sandwich has more blocks than parameters, of a length that holds the dependence.
- [ ] A Laplace mixture has `k_hat` at most 0.7.

# Profile Likelihood

[Back to Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/index.md)

A profile holds one parameter, or one prediction, at values that step away from the fit, and fits the other parameters again at each value. How fast the fit gets worse tells how well the data determine that quantity: the profile gives a confidence interval of each parameter and each prediction, and a verdict on its identifiability (Raue et al. 2009; Kreutz et al. 2012). Use it when the model is not linear in its parameters, where the intervals of a local approximation fail. Each profile refits with the problem's own optimizer, in parallel in Rust (`crates/commol-inference/src/profiles/`).

## Quick path

```python
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)
from commol.observations import NormalObservations
from commol.profiles import (
    PredictionProfile,
    PredictionSpec,
    ProfileLikelihood,
    Threshold,
)


def basic_model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# B every 4 steps up to step 40, with normal noise of sd 10.
truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=60)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
observations = [
    ObservedDataPoint(
        at=step,
        output="B",
        value=max(truth["B"][step] + rng.normal(0.0, 10.0), 0.0),
    )
    for step in range(4, 41, 4)
]
parameters = [
    CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
]
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=parameters,
    observation_models={"B": NormalObservations(sd=10.0)},
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000, sd_tolerance=1e-10),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(basic_model(None, None)), problem)

# The profile of each parameter, and its 95 % interval.
result = calibrator.uncertainty(
    ProfileLikelihood(parameters=["k1", "k2"], threshold=Threshold.chi_square(0.95))
)
for name in ("k1", "k2"):
    interval = result.intervals[name]
    print(name, round(interval.lower, 4), round(interval.upper, 4), result.verdicts[name])
# k1 0.3929 0.4055 identifiable
# k2 0.0984 0.104 identifiable

# The profile of B at step 20, inside the data, and at step 50, after them.
bands = calibrator.uncertainty(
    PredictionProfile(
        specs=[PredictionSpec(at=step, output="B", label=f"B at {step}") for step in (20, 50)],
        threshold=Threshold.chi_square(0.95),
    )
)
for label, interval in bands.intervals.items():
    print(label, round(interval.lower, 1), round(interval.upper, 1))
# B at 20 407.7 430.1
# B at 50 37.1 44.0
```

## How to read a profile

The **statistic** of a point is the objective of its refit less the objective of the fit: `−log L` with observation models, the loss otherwise. It is 0 at the fit and rises as the quantity moves away from it. The **interval** of the quantity is where the statistic stays below the **threshold**; each interval is pointwise, for one quantity at a time.

| Field of `ProfileResult` | Holds                                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `profiles[name]`         | A `Profile`: the `values`, the `statistics`, every parameter of each refit, the `threshold`, the `ends` of each side and the `evaluations` of the objective         |
| `intervals[name]`        | A `ProfileInterval`: `lower` and `upper`, `None` on a side that does not cross the threshold                                                                        |
| `verdicts[name]`         | What the shape says ([Verdicts](#verdicts-and-the-identifiability-report))                                                                                          |
| `fit`                    | The fit every profile starts from                                                                                                                                   |
| `tolerance`              | The numerical tolerance of the statistic, `max(τ, ν)` ([Verdicts](#verdicts-and-the-identifiability-report))                                                        |
| `structure`              | What resetting the other parameters says of each flat profile of a parameter (`ProfileStructure`)                                                                   |
| `notes`                  | A threshold below the tolerance, or a refit below the fit                                                                                                           |
| `failed`                 | With `Threshold.bootstrap_calibrated`, each replicate that failed, `"Replicate <index> failed: <reason>"`, also logged as a warning; empty with any other threshold |
| `not_converged`          | With `Threshold.bootstrap_calibrated`, the replicates kept although their optimizer did not converge                                                                |

| Shape                                             | Means                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A valley that crosses the threshold on both sides | The data determine the quantity; the interval is closed                        |
| A valley open on one side, up to a bound          | The data bound the quantity on one side only                                   |
| Flat over the whole range                         | The data cannot tell the values apart: another parameter makes up for this one |

A refit below the fit (a negative statistic) means that the fit is not the optimum; `notes` says so, and a fit with more starts (`starts=n`) fixes it.

```python
profile = result.profiles["k1"]
print(profile.ends, round(profile.threshold, 4))
# ('crossed', 'crossed') 1.9207
```

## Thresholds

The threshold is a required argument: it states what you assume about the noise.

| Threshold                                                     | Statistic                          | Assumes                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Threshold.chi_square(confidence_level)`                      | `−log L` of observation models     | The models hold, and `2 × statistic` is near `χ²₁` (Wilks); it gives `½ χ²₁(confidence_level)`. It needs observation models               |
| `Threshold.beale(confidence_level)`                           | A sum of squares, the loss `"sse"` | Independent Gaussian errors of one variance: `S(θ̂) · F(1, n − p; confidence_level) / (n − p)`, exact for a model linear in its parameters |
| `Threshold.bootstrap_calibrated(bootstrap, confidence_level)` | Any loss                           | That the bootstrap mimics how the data vary                                                                                               |

The bootstrap threshold calibrates the statistic itself (prepivoting, Beran 1988). Each replicate of `bootstrap` is the replicate `Calibrator.uncertainty(bootstrap)` makes from the problem's seed. Each replicate has two fits: a free one (`θ̂_b`), and one that holds the quantity at the value of the fit of the original data. The rise of the replicate is `PL_b(θ̂ⱼ) − L_b(θ̂_b)`. The threshold of the quantity is the quantile `confidence_level` of the rises, so each parameter gets its own. It costs one fit and one refit per quantity for each replicate. Any bootstrap of [Resampling](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/resampling/index.md) works, and the [parametric bootstrap](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/observation-models/#maximum-likelihood-against-the-posterior) with observation models.

```python
from commol.resampling import ResidualBootstrap

loss_problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=parameters,
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000, sd_tolerance=1e-10),
    seed=42,
)
loss_calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(basic_model(None, None)), loss_problem)
bootstrap = ResidualBootstrap(
    replicates=100, block_length=1, residual_scale="additive", scheme="moving"
)
for threshold in (
    Threshold.beale(0.95),
    Threshold.bootstrap_calibrated(bootstrap, 0.95),
):
    profiled = loss_calibrator.uncertainty(
        ProfileLikelihood(parameters=["k1"], threshold=threshold)
    )
    interval = profiled.intervals["k1"]
    print(threshold.kind, round(interval.lower, 4), round(interval.upper, 4))
# beale 0.3858 0.4129
# bootstrap_calibrated 0.3886 0.41
```

`Threshold.chi_square` on a problem with a loss raises a `ValueError` that names the other two; `Threshold.beale` on another loss, or on observation models, raises one too.

## How a profile is traced

| Step                | Rule                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Start               | The fit of `Calibrator.run(starts)`                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| Step                | The adaptive step of Raue et al. (2009): it starts at 1 % of the width of the bounds (of the value at the fit, for a prediction), doubles while a step rises by less than half of 10 % of the threshold, and halves when a step rises by more than twice it |
| Start of each refit | Every parameter extrapolated along the line through the two points before, as in Data2Dynamics                                                                                                                                                              |
| End of a side       | Past the threshold (`"crossed"`), at a bound (`"bound"`), after `max_steps` points (`"max_steps"`), or at a prediction no values within the bounds give (`"unreachable"`)                                                                                   |

Every side of every quantity runs in parallel. A held parameter leaves the values the optimizer searches, so Nelder-Mead searches one dimension less. A held prediction `g(θ) = c` is met as an equality constraint, by an augmented Lagrangian whose inner solver is the problem's optimizer. Its final multiplier is minus the slope of the profile (`Profile.multipliers`). With a particle swarm, each refit draws from a seed of its own, derived from the problem's seed, so a profile repeats; a swarm runs each outer iteration of a held prediction to its `max_iterations`, or until one of its [stop rules](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/calibration-optimizers/#stop-rules) holds.

## Prediction profiles

`PredictionProfile(specs, threshold)` profiles the value of each prediction: a `PredictionSpec` reads an output, or a sum of outputs, at a position, with a `window` and a `factor_id`, as an observation does. Its interval is the set of values the data do not reject (Kreutz et al. 2012); specs at several positions give a band. A prediction past the data has a wider interval, as `B at 50` shows in the [quick path](#quick-path). The intervals are pointwise: a band of them is not a joint region.

## Verdicts and the identifiability report

| Verdict                         | The profile                                                                                                       | In the report                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `identifiable`                  | Crosses the threshold on both sides                                                                               | Practical `determined`                                                                                                       |
| `practically_non_identifiable`  | Stays below on at least one side, up to a bound or `max_steps`                                                    | Practical `poorly_determined`                                                                                                |
| `structurally_non_identifiable` | Flat within `tolerance` over its whole range inside the box of the parameters, or proven flat by the resets below | Structural `in_combination` or `non_identifiable` from the resets; with no structural verdict, practical `poorly_determined` |

`tolerance` is `ε = max(τ, ν)`. `τ` is the `sd_tolerance` of Nelder-Mead, an absolute amount: argmin stops when the costs of its simplex spread by less. For a particle swarm with the improvement stop rule, `τ` is the improvement the rule allows at the fit, `tol_abs + tol_rel · |objective at the fit|`: the swarm stops when its best value improves by less. A swarm without that rule has no tolerance on the objective, and `τ` is `1e-6 · max(1, |objective at the fit|)`. `ν`, the noise floor, is the error of one evaluation of the objective at the fit, from the accuracy of a run: `Σ |∂ℓᵢ/∂mᵢ| · eᵢ`, with `eᵢ = rtol · |mᵢ| + k · atol` the error of a run on an observation that sums `k` outputs, its prediction `mᵢ`, and the accuracy of the engine (machine epsilon for a difference model, the `rtol` and `atol` of the ODE solver). A solver holds its tolerances at each step, so `ν` is an estimate, not a bound. A threshold at or below `ε` gives no verdict: the profile cannot tell a rise from numerical error, and `notes` says so.

The box of the parameters is the space inside their bounds. A free parameter of a refit is on a bound when it is within `1e-8` of the width of its bounds, or of the larger of 1 and the size of its one finite bound, the rule of the [local approximations](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/local/index.md). When it is on a bound that it is not on at the fit, the refit has left the box: the bound makes its rise, not the data. The flatness reads only the points inside the box, and a note names the parameter and the value where the ridge leaves it. When the crossing point of a side has such a parameter, and the parameter is not on that bound over the whole side, the side crosses because of the box. It counts as open, and its interval end stays, with a note. A parameter on its bound at every point from the fit to the crossing does not count: the verdict then holds within the box.

A profile is flat for one of two reasons: other parameters compensate the parameter along it, or nothing the data read depends on it. Raue et al. (2009) read such relations from the paths of the profiles. To tell them apart with no optimizer, each *reset* puts the parameter at one value of its profile inside the box, or at one end of its box, and every other parameter at its fitted value. Each reset evaluates the objective once and compares it with the objective at the fit, `f̂`. The evaluation floor `2(ν₁ + ν₂) + 2γₙ Σ|ℓᵢ|` (`ProfileResult.evaluation_floor`) is how far two evaluations can differ: `ν₁` is `ν`, `ν₂ = Σ ½ |ℓᵢ''| · eᵢ²` uses the expected curvature of each term (an estimate for a model that is not normal), and `γₙ · Σ |ℓᵢ|` bounds the rounding of the sum of the `n` terms, with the constants of `−log L`.

| Resets                                                                                                                        | Structural verdict                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Every reset feasible and within the floor of `f̂`                                                                              | `non_identifiable`, unless another parameter sits on its bound at the fit; the profile then reads `structurally_non_identifiable` |
| A flat profile with a feasible reset inside the box above `f̂ + T`                                                             | `in_combination`                                                                                                                  |
| Otherwise, a profile below the fit by more than the floor, no floor (a loss with no term derivatives), or a stochastic engine | None: practical `poorly_determined` for a flat profile, and a note                                                                |

A reset whose evaluation fails counts as infeasible. The ends of the box only rule out `non_identifiable`. A parameter is named in the reason when resetting it alone, where it moves most along the profile, raises the objective of that point above `T`; the parameters not named are then reset together, and a rise above the floor says that the list may be incomplete. Noise parameters of observation models are never named. `combinations` stays empty for a profile: it holds the algebraic combinations of the structural rank. Every reason says that the verdict holds with the other parameters at their fitted values. `Profile.refit_error` is the distance of a refit at the fit from `f̂`, a diagnostic of the optimizer, with a note when it is above `ε`.

What the settings give: with Nelder-Mead at its default `sd_tolerance` (`1e-6`), the resets prove a parameter with no effect `non_identifiable` on a difference model and on an ODE model at the default solver tolerances. A ridge needs its profile flat within `ε`: on an ODE model at the default tolerances `ν` is near `1e-4` and the profiles of the ridge below read `in_combination`; on a difference model `ν` is near `1e-13`, a refit lands about `1e-6` from its minimum, and the profile reads practically non-identifiable. Its `in_combination` needs an `sd_tolerance` near `ν`, as the example below uses.

`ProfileIdentifiability(result=profiles)` (`commol.identifiability`), run through `Calibrator.identifiability`, turns the verdicts into an [identifiability report](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/identifiability/#the-report) with a `profile` section, which `merge` joins with the other methods. A rate that reads `k1 * s` cannot tell `k1` from `s`: their profiles are flat on the ridge `k1 · s = constant`, resetting `s` breaks it, and the profile of `k1` reads `in_combination`, compensated by `s`, as the structural rank does. The two still disagree in some cases, and the merged verdict is then `conflicting`:

- the rank reads the rank most points of a Latin hypercube across the whole box have, a profile one ridge through the fit;
- the rank calls a parameter non-identifiable when its projection on the null space is above 0.95, and identifiable below 0.05: in a sum `k1 + k2` with `k1 ≫ k2`, the rank finds `k2` non-identifiable while its profile, which `k1` compensates, reads `in_combination`;
- a parameter with no effect while the others sit at their fit, but an effect elsewhere in the box, is `non_identifiable` for the profile, and may be identifiable for the rank.

```python
from commol.identifiability import ProfileIdentifiability, StructuralRank


def product_model(k1: float | None, s: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Product")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="s", value=s)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * s * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


product_problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.2, max_bound=0.8),
        CalibrationParameter(id="s", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.5, max_bound=2.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    observation_models={"B": NormalObservations(sd=10.0)},
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=4000, sd_tolerance=1e-15),
    seed=42,
)
product = Calibrator(Simulation(product_model(None, None, None)), product_problem)
profiles = product.uncertainty(
    ProfileLikelihood(parameters=["k1"], threshold=Threshold.chi_square(0.95))
)
print(profiles.verdicts)
# {'k1': 'structurally_non_identifiable'}
print(profiles.notes[0])
# 'k1': the ridge leaves the box at 0.8 above the fit, where 's' reaches its
# bound; the profile is flat inside the box, and its rise past it comes from
# the bounds, not the data.
print(profiles.structure["k1"].compensated_by)  # ['s']
report = product.identifiability(StructuralRank(points=5, design="observations"))
merged = report.merge(
    product.identifiability(ProfileIdentifiability(result=profiles))
)
print(merged.verdicts["k1"].structural.verdict, merged.verdicts["s"].structural.verdict)
# in_combination in_combination
```

## Plots

`result.plot()` draws one panel per profile: the statistic of each point, the threshold as a dashed line and the ends of the interval as dotted lines. Like every figure of commol, it returns the matplotlib `Figure` and takes `output_file`, `config` and `axes` ([Plotting](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#plotting)).

```python
figure = result.plot()
```

## Checklist

- [ ] The threshold states your noise: `chi_square` with observation models, `beale` for a sum of squares of independent Gaussian errors, `bootstrap_calibrated` otherwise.
- [ ] No note says that a refit went below the fit; if one does, fit with more starts.
- [ ] Every verdict is set; a threshold below the tolerance needs data with noise, or a tighter `sd_tolerance`.
- [ ] For `in_combination` on a difference model, `sd_tolerance` is near the noise floor `ν` (`notes` says why a flat profile has no structural verdict, and when a refit is less accurate than the tolerance).
- [ ] A side that ends at `max_steps` is open only because it stopped: raise `max_steps`.
- [ ] Read an open or flat profile with the [structural rank](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/identifiability/#structural-rank) before you call a parameter non-identifiable.

# Conformal Prediction Intervals

[Back to Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/index.md)

Conformal prediction gives intervals for observations, with a coverage guarantee that needs no noise model, no prior and no correct model. It answers "will the next observations fall inside?", not "which parameters fit?". Each variant scores how far observations the fit did not use fall from their predictions, and a quantile of those scores sets the width of every interval. Use it when you must state how often new data fall inside an interval, and you cannot or will not say how the data scatter around the model. Every variant runs through `Calibrator.uncertainty`, in Rust (`crates/commol-inference/src/conformal/`).

## Quick path

```python
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)
from commol.conformal import SplitConformal


def ab_model(k: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="AB")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_parameter(id="k", value=k)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# Noisy data of B at steps 1 to 80: fit steps 1 to 40, hold out 41 to 80.
truth = Simulation(ab_model(0.05)).run(num_steps=90)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
observations = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step] + rng.normal(0.0, 5.0))
    for step in range(1, 81)
]
fitted = [point for point in observations if point.at <= 40]
held_out = [point for point in observations if point.at > 40]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=fitted,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=0.5)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(ab_model(None)), problem)

result = calibrator.uncertainty(
    SplitConformal(
        calibration_data=held_out,
        score="absolute",
        by="series",
        confidence_level=0.9,
        positions=[85.0, 90.0],
    )
)
intervals = result.intervals.series["B"]
print([round(value, 1) for value in intervals.lower])  # [981.0, 983.9]
print([round(value, 1) for value in intervals.upper])  # [993.4, 996.3]
print(result.guarantee)
```

`result.intervals` holds the intervals of each series at `positions`, `result.scores` the scores they came from, and `result.guarantee` what the coverage claim assumes.

## What the guarantee means

A conformal interval of level `1 − α` covers a **new observation** with probability at least `1 − α`, averaged over the data and the new observation.

| It says                                                                      | It does not say                                                                 |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Of many new observations, at least a share `1 − α` falls inside its interval | That one interval holds its observation with probability `1 − α` given the data |
| The claim holds whatever the noise, and even when the model is wrong         | That the interval contains the model curve or the true parameters               |
| A wrong model gives wide intervals, not wrong ones                           | That the intervals are narrow                                                   |

The claim holds when the scores are **exchangeable**: any order of the scores of the held-out and the new observations is as likely as any other. Noise that is independent and of one distribution along the series is exchangeable; a trend in the errors, a change of regime, or errors that depend on each other are not. Each variant names its assumption in `result.guarantee`.

The quantile of `n` scores at level `1 − α` is the `⌈(n + 1)(1 − α)⌉`-th smallest (`conformal_quantile` in `crates/commol-inference/src/conformal/quantile.rs`). With fewer than `1/α − 1` scores that rank is above `n`, so the interval is unbounded: `-inf` to `inf`. `result.intervals.unbounded` names the positions of each series where that happens. At level 0.9 a quantile needs 9 scores.

## Scores and pooling

Every variant takes a `score`, a `by` and a `confidence_level`, none with a default: they change the width of the intervals, which is a modelling choice.

| `score`        | Score of `y` against `ŷ` | Interval | Use it when                                                                              |
| -------------- | ------------------------ | -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `"absolute"`   | \`                       | y − ŷ    | \`                                                                                       |
| `"normalized"` | \`                       | y − ŷ    | / s`, with `s\` the root mean square of the observed values of the series in the problem |
| `"spread"`     | \`                       | y − ŷ    | / σ̂`, with `σ̂\` the spread of the predictions at that point                              |

`by="series"` gives each series (observation label) its own quantile; `by="all"` gives every series one quantile. Per series is the safer first choice: a small series does not borrow the errors of a large one, but it needs `1/α − 1` scores of its own.

- `score="normalized"` with `by="series"` raises a `ValueError`: with one constant factor per series, its intervals are those of `"absolute"`.
- `score="spread"` needs predictions with a spread. `SplitConformal` and `AdaptiveConformal` take it from a `sample`, whose predictive gives the prediction (its weighted median) and the spread (its weighted standard deviation); without one they raise a `ValueError`. `JackknifePlus` and `EnbPI` take it from their own refits. `RollingConformal` fits once per origin, so it rejects `"spread"`.

```python
from commol.uncertainty import ParameterSample, SampleMethod

sample = ParameterSample.equally_weighted(
    names=["k"],
    bounds=[(0.0, 0.5)],
    values=[[0.048], [0.05], [0.052]],
    method=SampleMethod(name="by hand"),
)
spread = calibrator.uncertainty(
    SplitConformal(
        calibration_data=held_out,
        score="spread",
        by="series",
        confidence_level=0.9,
        positions=[85.0, 90.0],
        sample=sample,
    )
)
widths = [
    round(upper - lower, 1)
    for lower, upper in zip(spread.intervals.series["B"].lower, spread.intervals.series["B"].upper)
]
print(widths)  # [6.3, 5.2]
```

## Which variant to use

| Variant             | Held-out data                               | Fits           | Guarantee                                                                                               | Use it for                                                         |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `SplitConformal`    | `calibration_data`                          | One            | At least `1 − α`, exchangeable scores                                                                   | Many observations, some of which you can leave out of the fit      |
| `RollingConformal`  | None: each origin holds out what follows it | One per origin | At least `1 − α` per horizon, scores of a horizon exchangeable across origins                           | Forecasts: intervals ahead of the data that widen with the horizon |
| `JackknifePlus`     | None                                        | One per block  | At least `1 − 2α` with one observation per block; the CV+ bound with longer blocks; exchangeable blocks | Short series, where no data can be spared                          |
| `EnbPI`             | None                                        | `replicates`   | Near `1 − α`, approximately, under stationary and strongly mixing errors                                | Time series with dependent errors                                  |
| `AdaptiveConformal` | The `stream` of new observations            | One            | The long-run share of misses tends to `α`, with no assumption                                           | Data that arrive one by one and can change regime                  |

## How to hold data out

| Variant                  | What to hold out                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SplitConformal`         | Pass the problem the observations to fit, and `calibration_data` the rest. For a forecast, hold out the latest positions, as in the quick path, so the scores measure errors ahead of the fit. The held-out points must not be in the problem. |
| `RollingConformal`       | Nothing: give `origins`. Each fits the observations at or before it and scores the later ones, so the problem holds every observation.                                                                                                         |
| `JackknifePlus`, `EnbPI` | Nothing: they leave blocks out of their own refits. A block holds every observation of every series at `block_length` consecutive positions, so dependence stays inside a block.                                                               |
| `AdaptiveConformal`      | The observations that arrive after the fit, in `stream`.                                                                                                                                                                                       |

## Split conformal

`SplitConformal(calibration_data, score, by, confidence_level, positions, sample=None, starts=1)` fits the problem's observations (`Calibrator.run(starts)`), or reads a `sample`, scores `calibration_data` and gives intervals at `positions` for each series of `calibration_data`. A series of `calibration_data` is read as its observations define it: its outputs, factor and window.

## Rolling origins

`RollingConformal(origins, score, by, confidence_level, positions, starts=1)` gives intervals ahead of the data, with one quantile per horizon. Horizon `k` is the `k`-th observation of a series after an origin: a count, not a distance on the axis, because positions can be irregular. Each origin fits the observations at or before it (one refit per origin, from the fit of every observation) and scores the later ones. The intervals are around the fit of every observation, at `positions`, which must all be after the data; the `k`-th position is horizon `k`, so give positions spaced as the observations. A horizon with fewer than `1/α − 1` origins that reach it has an unbounded interval.

```python
from commol.conformal import RollingConformal

every_point = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=problem.parameters,
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator_all = Calibrator(Simulation(ab_model(None)), every_point)
rolling = calibrator_all.uncertainty(
    RollingConformal(
        origins=[float(step) for step in range(30, 71)],
        score="absolute",
        by="series",
        confidence_level=0.8,
        positions=[81.0, 82.0, 83.0],
    )
)
print(rolling.intervals.unbounded)  # {}
```

## Jackknife+

`JackknifePlus(block_length, score, by, confidence_level, positions, starts=1)` refits once per block left out (Barber et al. 2021). Observation `i` of block `b` has the residual `Rᵢ` of the fit `μ̂₋ᵦ` that left its block out, and the interval at a point `x` is

```text
[ q⁻_α { μ̂₋ᵦ₍ᵢ₎(x) − Rᵢ } ,  q⁺_{1−α} { μ̂₋ᵦ₍ᵢ₎(x) + Rᵢ } ]
```

where `q⁺` is the `⌈(1 − α)(n + 1)⌉`-th smallest value and `q⁻` the `⌊α(n + 1)⌋`-th smallest. The guarantee holds with no held-out set, under exchangeable blocks. With `n` scored observations in `K` blocks it is the bound of K-fold CV+ (Theorem 4):

```text
1 − 2α − min{ 2(1 − 1/K) / (n/K + 1),  (1 − K/n) / (K + 1) }
```

With one observation per block, `K = n` and the bound is `1 − 2α`. With longer blocks, jackknife+ is CV+ with the blocks as folds, so CV+ has no class of its own. The theorem assumes blocks of `n/K` observations each. `cv_plus_bound` in `crates/commol-inference/src/conformal/jackknife_plus.rs` computes it, and `result.guarantee` states it.

```python
from commol.conformal import JackknifePlus

jackknife = calibrator.uncertainty(
    JackknifePlus(block_length=4, score="absolute", by="series", confidence_level=0.9, positions=[45.0])
)
print(jackknife.guarantee)  # ... at least 0.7318 ... with K = 10 blocks of 4 positions ...
```

## EnbPI

`EnbPI(replicates, block_length, score, by, confidence_level, positions, starts=1)` draws its own replicates (Xu and Xie 2021): each draws as many blocks as there are, with replacement, and fits with each observation's weight multiplied by the count of its block, so the blocks it did not draw get weight 0. The leave-one-out prediction of an observation is the mean of the replicates that left its block out; the point prediction at a position is the mean of the leave-one-out predictions there. No fit beyond the replicates is needed. A block left out by no replicate raises a `ValueError` that asks for more replicates: a block is left out by a replicate with probability about `1/e ≈ 0.37`.

## Adaptive conformal inference

`AdaptiveConformal(confidence_level, step, score, by, stream, sample=None, starts=1)` walks the observations of `stream` in order of position (Gibbs and Candès 2021). The interval of each point is the quantile, at the working level `1 − α_t`, of the scores of the earlier points of the stream; then the point is scored and the working level moves:

```text
α_{t+1} = α_t + γ (α − err_t),   err_t = 1 for a miss, 0 for a cover
```

So a miss widens the next interval and a cover narrows it. The long-run share of misses tends to `α` whatever the data. `by="series"` keeps one working level per series, `by="all"` one for all. The first points have few earlier scores, so their intervals are unbounded. `result.intervals` holds the interval given at each point before it was seen.

```python
from commol.conformal import AdaptiveConformal

adaptive = calibrator.uncertainty(
    AdaptiveConformal(confidence_level=0.9, step=0.05, score="absolute", by="series", stream=held_out)
)
series = adaptive.intervals.series["B"]
misses = [
    not lower <= point.value <= upper
    for lower, upper, point in zip(series.lower, series.upper, held_out)
]
print(len(adaptive.intervals.unbounded["B"]))  # 7
print(round(sum(misses) / len(misses), 3))  # 0.125
```

## Results, plots and reports

Every variant returns a `ConformalResult(intervals, scores, guarantee, failed, not_converged, block_length, block_length_estimates)`. A variant that refits lists each refit that failed in `failed`, named by its unit: `"Origin <index> failed: <reason>"` for `RollingConformal`, `"Block <index> failed: <reason>"` for `JackknifePlus`, and `"Replicate <index> failed: <reason>"` for `EnbPI`; each is also logged as a warning, and gives no score. `not_converged` counts the refits kept although their optimizer did not converge. Split and adaptive conformal do not refit, so their `failed` is empty and their `not_converged` is 0. `JackknifePlus` and `EnbPI` give the block length they ran with in `block_length`, and with `block_length="auto"` the estimate of each series, by label, in `block_length_estimates`, as the [bootstraps](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/resampling/#blocks-and-their-length) give them; the other variants have no blocks, so both are `None`. `intervals` is a `PredictionIntervals`: its `confidence_level`, a `SeriesIntervals` per series (`positions`, `prediction`, `lower`, `upper`), and `unbounded`. `plot.series(prediction_intervals=...)` of a run, of replicates or of a predictive draws the band of each series on its panel. `SimulationResults.report`, `SimulationReplicates.report` and `Predictive.report` take `prediction_intervals=...` too, and add the intervals under the key `prediction_intervals`.

```python
run = Simulation(ab_model(0.05)).run(num_steps=90)
figure = run.plot.series(
    observed_data=observations, prediction_intervals=result.intervals, series=["B"]
)
```

## Checklist

- [ ] The held-out observations are not in the problem, and come from where the new observations will.
- [ ] Each quantile has at least `1/α − 1` scores; `result.intervals.unbounded` is empty.
- [ ] The assumption in `result.guarantee` fits your data: exchangeable scores, mixing errors, or none.
- [ ] For a forecast, you use `RollingConformal`, `EnbPI` or `AdaptiveConformal`, not one split of errors one step ahead.

| Bootstraps and the jackknife of the parameters                                   | [Resampling](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/resampling/index.md)                                                                                              |
