# Sensitivity Analysis

[Back to Uncertainty](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/index.md)

A sensitivity analysis asks the forward questions of a model: how uncertainty in its inputs moves its outputs, and which inputs matter most. It needs no data. You say what varies and how (an `InputSpace`), what to read from each run (quantities of interest), and a method: Monte Carlo propagation, partial rank correlation (PRCC), Morris screening, Sobol indices or a polynomial chaos expansion. Every method runs through `SensitivityAnalysis(simulation, inputs).run(method)`, in one call into Rust: the design (`crates/commol-inference/src/design.rs`), the runs (`batch.rs`) and the estimator (`global_sensitivity/`), joined by `ForwardAnalysis` (`global_sensitivity/analysis.rs`).

## Quick path

```python
from commol import Aggregate, CalibrationParameter, ModelBuilder, Simulation
from commol.sensitivity import InputSpace, PRCC, SensitivityAnalysis
from commol.distributions import Normal, Uniform
from commol.quantities import Peak


def abc_model(k1: float, k2: float):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="ABC")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


simulation = Simulation(abc_model(0.3, 0.1))
inputs = InputSpace.independent(
    [
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.2, max_bound=0.6),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.05, max_bound=0.2),
    ],
    {"k1": Uniform(), "k2": Normal(mean=0.1, sd=0.03)},
)
analysis = SensitivityAnalysis(simulation, inputs, seed=1)

peak = Peak(series="B", positions=list(range(101)))
result = analysis.run(PRCC(draws=200, quantities=[peak]))
print(result.inputs, [round(c, 2) for c in result.coefficients[0]])  # ['k1', 'k2'] [0.97, -0.95]
```

The peak of `B` rises with `k1` and falls with `k2`: the PRCC of `k1` is near 1 and that of `k2` near −1. Over the axis (below), `C` early on rises with both, since a faster flow out of `B` fills `C` faster, and late falls with `k2`, since a faster flow out of `B` ends the growth of `B` sooner.

## Forward and inverse questions

| Question                                                            | Needs data | Entry point                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Which inputs fit the data, and how well do the data determine them? | Yes        | `Calibrator.run`, `Calibrator.uncertainty`, `Calibrator.identifiability`      |
| How does uncertainty in the inputs move the outputs?                | No         | `SensitivityAnalysis.run(Propagation(...))`                                   |
| Which inputs matter most for an output?                             | No         | `SensitivityAnalysis.run` with `PRCC`, `Morris`, `Sobol` or `PolynomialChaos` |

The two meet: a sample that a calibration returns, such as a posterior, can be the input space of an analysis (`InputSpace.from_sample`).

## What varies

Each input is a `CalibrationParameter`: a model parameter or an initial condition, with its bounds, as a calibration sets it. The values reach the engine as a calibration writes them (`ForwardModel::unobserved`, `crates/commol-calibration/src/forward.rs`).

| Constructor                                         | Inputs                                                                                                                                                                                       | Methods that take it     |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `InputSpace.independent(parameters, distributions)` | One distribution per input (`Uniform()`, `LogUniform()`, `Beta(a, b)`, `Normal(mean, sd)`, `LogNormal(mu, sigma)`, `Gamma(shape, rate)`), truncated to its bounds, independent of the others | Every method             |
| `InputSpace.uniform_on_bounds(parameters)`          | `Uniform()` on the bounds of every input; they must be finite                                                                                                                                | Every method             |
| `InputSpace.from_sample(sample, parameters)`        | The draws of a `ParameterSample`, with their weights; the inputs may depend on each other. The parameters give the type of each value, which a sample does not hold                          | `Propagation` and `PRCC` |

An initial condition is an amount in the unit of its bin, or a category split in `[0, 1]`, with `initial_condition_remainder` as in a calibration problem. A factor or a noise parameter is not an input: both belong to observations, and an analysis has none.

`SensitivityAnalysis(simulation, inputs, *, replicates=None, seed=None)` holds the inputs for every method you run on it. With a stochastic engine `replicates` (at least 1) and `seed` are required. A point of the design of PRCC, Morris, Sobol or a polynomial chaos runs `replicates` replicates, on the same seeds at every point, and holds their mean: the indices are those of the mean of `replicates` replicates, and they come close to those of the expected value as `replicates` grows. A propagation, and the `Predictive` of its draws, keep every replicate, each with a seed of its own. A deterministic engine does not use `replicates`, so the same analysis runs on either engine; with no seed, the engine draws one, which `analysis.seed` gives and the analysis logs. A negative `replicates` raises `ValueError` that names the setting.

## Quantities of interest

A quantity reads a series of each run and reduces it to a scalar, in Rust, through the observation operator of the calibration (`crates/commol-inference/src/quantity.rs`), so a design of thousands of runs never returns to Python. The quantities live in `commol/quantities/quantities.py`.

| Series                                       | Value at a position                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A name, a list of names, or `Level(outputs)` | The sum of the outputs, their level                                                                    |
| `Increments(outputs, window)`                | The gain of the sum over `(end - window, end]`: the position is the end of a window, at least `window` |

| Quantity                                        | Value                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `ValueAt(series, at)`                           | The value at `at`                                                                                                                    |
| `Peak(series, positions)`                       | The largest value at the positions                                                                                                   |
| `PeakPosition(series, positions)`               | The first of the positions where the value is largest                                                                                |
| `Trajectory(series, positions)`                 | The value at each position, one scalar per position, for an analysis over the axis                                                   |
| `Gain(outputs, start, end)`                     | The value at `end` minus the value at `start`: what entered a cumulative output over `(start, end]`, as an observation with a window |
| `Ratio(numerator, denominator, replicate_rule)` | One quantity of one value over another, in each run ([A ratio of two quantities](#a-ratio-of-two-quantities))                        |

The series is a modelling choice. The peak of a level is the largest amount; for an output that only grows, such as `C` here or an accumulator, it is the value at the last position. The peak of `Increments` is the largest gain over one window, and `PeakPosition` gives the end of that window:

```python
from commol.quantities import Increments, PeakPosition
from commol.sensitivity import Propagation

ends = list(range(10, 101, 10))
inflow = Increments("C", window=10)
quantities = [
    Peak(series=inflow, positions=ends),
    PeakPosition(series=inflow, positions=ends),
    Peak(series="C", positions=ends),
]
gains = analysis.run(Propagation(draws=100, quantities=quantities))
for summary in gains.summary(0.9):
    print(summary.label, round(summary.lower), round(summary.median), round(summary.upper))
# peak of C gain over windows of 10 178 358 496
# position of the peak of C gain over windows of 10 20 30 50
# peak of C 809 980 999
```

Every quantity follows the same rules:

| Rule                                                                       | So                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A quantity reads only the positions it names, with no interpolation        | A position the engine does not report at is a `ValueError`                                                                 |
| Outputs are summed at each row before any reduction                        | The peak of `["A", "B"]` is the peak of `A + B`                                                                            |
| `PeakPosition` gives the first of the positions where the value is largest | A tie gives the earlier position                                                                                           |
| A NaN in a value a quantity reads makes it NaN                             | Its peak and the position of its peak are NaN too                                                                          |
| With a stochastic engine, a quantity is computed for each replicate        | A design point holds the mean of its replicates, or for a `Ratio` what its `replicate_rule` says; a propagation keeps each |

Each quantity has a `label`, by default what it reads, such as `"B at 10"`. The default label writes each position in full, as Python reads it back, so two positions give two labels: `"B at 1000000"` and `"B at 1000001"`.

### A quantity that is NaN

A propagation keeps the NaN of each run in `values`. Every reduction across runs raises a `ValueError` on a NaN: `summary()`, `member_statistics`, and PRCC, Morris, Sobol and the polynomial chaos at the first batch of their design, before they estimate. The message gives the index of the quantity, in the order of the labels, the points where it is NaN, and the first run: its point, inputs, replicate and seed. A `Propagation` with the same inputs and seed gives the value of each run.

`PropagationResult.where(mask)` keeps the runs where `mask` is true and renormalises their weights to sum to 1. A filter conditions the result: the summary is the distribution given the condition, not over every run, and `effective_size` says how many runs the kept weights are worth. You write the condition, such as `np.isfinite(values[:, i])` or a value above a threshold:

```python
import numpy as np

values = np.asarray(gains.values)
late = gains.where(values[:, 1] > 30)
print(len(late.values), round(late.effective_size), round(gains.effective_size))  # 23 23 100
print(round(late.summary(0.9)[0].median))  # 216
```

### A ratio of two quantities

`Ratio(numerator, denominator, replicate_rule)` divides two quantities of one value each (`ValueAt`, `Gain`, `Peak`), numerator N over denominator D, in each run. It is one quantity, so every method reads it, the sensitivity methods too. A `PeakPosition` or a `Trajectory` as an operand is a `ValueError`. The share of what entered `C` by position 100 that entered by position 50 has a denominator that depends on both inputs:

```python
from commol.quantities import Gain, Ratio

early = Ratio(
    numerator=Gain(outputs="C", start=0, end=50),
    denominator=Gain(outputs="C", start=0, end=100),
    replicate_rule="within",
    label="early share",
)
spread = analysis.run(Propagation(draws=100, quantities=[early]))
share = spread.summary(0.9)[0]
print(share.label, round(share.lower, 2), round(share.median, 2), round(share.upper, 2))
# early share 0.61 0.94 0.99
ranked = analysis.run(PRCC(draws=200, quantities=[early]))
print(ranked.inputs, [round(c, 2) for c in ranked.coefficients[0]])  # ['k1', 'k2'] [0.92, 0.69]
```

The default label is `"(N) / (D)"`, from the labels of the two quantities. `replicate_rule` is required, with no default: with a stochastic engine, it says how the replicates of a point of PRCC, Morris, Sobol or a polynomial chaos combine (`Quantities::combine` in `crates/commol-inference/src/quantity.rs`). They are three estimands, and the choice is yours:

| `replicate_rule`    | Value of a point                                           | No value when         |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `"within"`          | The mean of the ratio of each replicate, E[N/D]            | A replicate has D = 0 |
| `"within_positive"` | The mean of the ratio of the replicates with D > 0, E\[N/D | D > 0\]               |
| `"pooled"`          | The ratio of the means, E[N]/E[D]                          | E[D] = 0              |

A deterministic engine has one run per point, so the three give N/D. A `Propagation`, `Scenarios` and the quantities of one run keep the ratio of each run, N/D, for each replicate.

| Rule                                                       | So                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The ratio of a run with D = 0 is NaN, also when N is not 0 | N/0 is not ±inf, which a check for NaN misses; the NaN rule of [A quantity that is NaN](#a-quantity-that-is-nan) holds in every method                                                          |
| A point with no value is NaN in every method               | The error names the point and its inputs, and the replicate that is NaN, when one is                                                                                                            |
| `"within"` with D = 0 in one replicate                     | The point has no value. A Sobol design of 10^5 replicates almost surely holds one such replicate when D can reach 0                                                                             |
| `"within_positive"`                                        | It conditions on D > 0, so it hides the effect of an input on the chance that D > 0: analyse that chance on its own. Its points average different numbers of replicates, so their noise differs |
| `"pooled"`                                                 | The ratio of two means is another quantity than the mean of the ratios: it differs from `"within"` when D is small or 0 in some replicates                                                      |

The indices of a ratio equal those of its numerator only when the denominator is fixed and is not an input, such as the sum of the bins at 0: then run the method on the numerator. When the denominator can be near 0, a ratio has large values in a few runs, and the Sobol and the chaos indices, which divide variances, are unstable; PRCC works on ranks, so it stays valid.

A propagation keeps the NaN of each run in `values`, so `summary()` raises on a ratio with D = 0 in a run. `PropagationResult.where` keeps the runs where the ratio is finite, and the summary is then conditioned on that.

### The quantities of one run

`results.quantities(quantities)` reduces one run to its quantities, as `dict[str, float]` with one value per label, and `replicates.quantities(quantities)` gives one such dict per replicate, in seed order, with no mean. Use them on the point estimate of a fit, or on any run you plot; `predictive.quantities(quantities)` gives one dict per draw of a predictive, and `Scenarios` compares them between scenarios ([Scenarios](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#scenarios)). Rust reads the rows of the run at the positions of the quantities and reduces them with the code of `Propagation` (`Quantities::evaluate_run` in `crates/commol-inference/src/quantity.rs`), so the values equal those of a `Propagation` of a sample of one draw with the parameters of the run.

`quantity_schedule(quantities)` gives the positions the quantities read: the results of `run_at` at them hold every position. Each position is found within a relative tolerance of `1e-9`, as `index_at` finds it, so a window that starts at `0.3 - 0.1` reads the row of `0.2`.

```python
from commol.quantities import quantity_schedule

one_run = simulation.run_at(quantity_schedule(quantities))
for label, value in one_run.quantities(quantities).items():
    print(label, round(value))
# peak of C gain over windows of 10 283
# position of the peak of C gain over windows of 10 30
# peak of C 946
```

| Case                                               | Result                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The run lacks a position a quantity reads          | `ValueError` that lists each such position with its quantity, and says to call `Simulation.run_at`                                                                                                                                                       |
| A quantity names an output the results do not have | `ValueError` that names the output                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `run(n)` of the ODE engine                         | It interpolates the positions that are not breakpoints, so a value differs from that of a run that ends there by about the relative tolerance of the solver, and `PeakPosition` can change on a near-tie                                                 |
| The replicates of a stochastic engine              | Each replicate is reduced on its own. The runs of a draw follow the tree of seeds of a [predictive](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#the-predictive), from `result.draw_seeds`. The seed of the analysis itself gives other runs |

## Which method for which budget

| Method                                                                         | Answers                                                                                    | Runs                                                                                        | Inputs                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `Propagation(draws, quantities)`                                               | The distribution of each quantity, and the band of every output                            | `draws`; with inputs from a sample, `draws` is left unset and every draw of the sample runs | Independent or a sample |
| `PRCC(draws, quantities)`                                                      | How steadily each quantity rises or falls with each input                                  | `draws`, more than the inputs + 1; with inputs from a sample, as `Propagation`              | Independent or a sample |
| `Morris(trajectories, levels, quantities)`                                     | Which inputs matter, in few runs                                                           | `trajectories · (inputs + 1)`                                                               | Independent             |
| `Sobol(draws, replicates, confidence_level, quantities)`                       | The share of the variance each input explains, alone and with interactions, with intervals | `draws · (inputs + 2)`                                                                      | Independent             |
| `PolynomialChaos(degree, draws, quantities, q_norm=1.0, max_interaction=None)` | A polynomial surrogate and its Sobol indices, in far fewer runs for a smooth quantity      | `draws`, more than the terms                                                                | Independent             |

Start with Morris to drop the inputs that do not matter, then Sobol or a polynomial chaos on the rest. For a slow model, a polynomial chaos needs the fewest runs; read its leave-one-out error before its indices.

## Propagation

`Propagation` returns a `PropagationResult`: the `sample` of the draws (a Latin hypercube of the distributions, or the input sample as it is), the quantities of each run, their `weights`, and the seed of each draw (`draw_seeds`). `summary(confidence_level)` gives the weighted mean, median and central interval of each quantity. The sample is a `ParameterSample`, so `Predictive(analysis, result.sample, positions)` gives the bands and plots of a calibration.

```python
from commol.uncertainty import Predictive
from commol.sensitivity import Propagation
from commol.quantities import ValueAt

result = analysis.run(
    Propagation(draws=100, quantities=[peak, ValueAt(series="C", at=100)])
)
for summary in result.summary(0.9):
    print(summary.label, round(summary.lower), round(summary.median), round(summary.upper))
# peak of B 172 421 655
# C at 100 809 980 999

band = Predictive(analysis, result.sample, [0.0, 25.0, 50.0]).band(0.9)
print([round(value) for value in band.median["B"]])  # [10, 293, 53]
```

`Predictive.at_observations` of an analysis takes `NoNoise()` only: residual noise needs the residuals of a fit, and `DistributionNoise()` the observation models of a problem.

## PRCC

`PRCC` (Marino et al. 2008) ranks the inputs and each quantity, and gives the correlation of the rank of an input with the rank of the quantity once the other inputs are accounted for. A coefficient near 1 or −1 says the quantity rises or falls steadily with the input; near 0, that it does not. `p_values` test each coefficient against 0.

With inputs from a sample, the sample is the design, and the ranks, the correlations and the test read its weights: a rank is the weight below a value plus half the weight at it, and the test counts Kish's effective size in place of the draws. Equal weights give the usual PRCC. A `Trajectory` gives the coefficients over the axis; a quantity with one value in every run, such as a state at position 0, has NaN coefficients.

A NaN has no rank, so a quantity that is NaN at a draw raises a `ValueError` before PRCC ranks any value ([A quantity that is NaN](#a-quantity-that-is-nan)).

```python
from commol.quantities import Trajectory

over_axis = analysis.run(
    PRCC(draws=100, quantities=[Trajectory(series="C", positions=[10, 50, 100])])
)
print(over_axis.labels)  # ['C at 10', 'C at 50', 'C at 100']
print([[round(c, 2) for c in row] for row in over_axis.coefficients])
# [[0.99, 0.9], [0.91, 0.31], [0.96, -0.89]]
```

## Morris screening

`Morris` (Morris 1991) runs `trajectories` trajectories: each starts at a random level of every input and moves the inputs one at a time, by half the `levels`. The levels are the centres of strata of equal probability of each distribution, so a level is finite for an unbounded distribution too, and an effect is on the scale of `F(x)`, so inputs of different units compare. `mu_star` (Campolongo, Cariboni and Saltelli 2007) ranks the inputs; a `sigma` near or above `mu_star` says the effect depends on the other inputs or is not linear.

```python
from commol.sensitivity import Morris

screening = analysis.run(Morris(trajectories=20, levels=4, quantities=[peak]))
print([round(value) for value in screening.mu_star[0]], screening.runs)  # [385, 279] 60
```

## Sobol indices

`Sobol` uses the design of Saltelli (2010) on two matrices of independent Monte Carlo draws. The first-order index of an input (`first`) is the share of the variance of the quantity it explains alone; the total index (`total`) adds every interaction it takes part in, so `first ≤ total` up to the Monte Carlo error that the intervals show: below, the estimates of `k1` cross, and their intervals overlap. The intervals are percentiles of a bootstrap of the rows, at `confidence_level`.

Sobol, Morris and the polynomial chaos need independent inputs. With dependent inputs, such as a posterior, moving one input breaks its dependence on the others, and the indices lose their meaning and no longer add up; an input space from a sample raises a `ValueError` that names PRCC and propagation, which take it.

```python
from commol.sensitivity import Sobol

indices = analysis.run(
    Sobol(draws=1024, replicates=200, confidence_level=0.9, quantities=[peak])
)
for name, i in [("k1", 0), ("k2", 1)]:
    first = (indices.first_lower[0][i], indices.first[0][i], indices.first_upper[0][i])
    total = (indices.total_lower[0][i], indices.total[0][i], indices.total_upper[0][i])
    print(name, [round(s, 2) for s in first], [round(s, 2) for s in total])
# k1 [0.47, 0.63, 0.78] [0.55, 0.59, 0.63]
# k2 [0.21, 0.36, 0.48] [0.38, 0.41, 0.45]
```

## Polynomial chaos

`PolynomialChaos` (Sudret 2008) takes every input to `u = F(x)`, uniform on `[0, 1]`, and fits orthonormal Legendre polynomials of `u` of total degree `degree`, or a truncation of that basis ([below](#bases-for-many-inputs)), by least squares on a Latin hypercube of `draws` points. One basis fits every distribution, truncated ones too. The Sobol indices come from the squares of the coefficients. `loo_error` is the leave-one-out error relative to the variance: the indices are those of the expansion, and they are those of the model only as far as the expansion predicts it. `predict` gives the quantities at any input values, as a surrogate.

```python
from commol.sensitivity import PolynomialChaos

chaos = analysis.run(PolynomialChaos(degree=4, draws=60, quantities=[peak]))
print(round(chaos.loo_error[0], 4), [round(s, 2) for s in chaos.total[0]])  # 0.0036 [0.61, 0.39]
print([round(value) for value in chaos.predict([[0.4, 0.1]])[0]])  # [428]
```

### Bases for many inputs

The total-degree basis has `(k + degree)! / (k! degree!)` terms in `k` inputs: 10,626 for 20 inputs at degree 4. A fit needs more draws than terms, so a model of many inputs needs a smaller basis. You choose how to truncate it, with two keyword arguments:

| Argument          | Keeps                                                                                                                                                  | Default                 |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------- |
| `max_interaction` | The terms of at most this many inputs                                                                                                                  | `None`: no limit        |
| `q_norm`          | The terms whose degrees `α` have `Σ α_i^q ≤ degree^q`, with `q` in `(0, 1]`: below 1, a term of several inputs keeps a lower degree than a term of one | `1.0`: the total degree |

The defaults keep the total-degree basis. With `max_interaction=2`, 20 inputs at degree 4 have `1 + 20 · 4 + C(20, 2) · 6 = 1,221` terms. The number of terms is known before any run, so too few `draws` raise before the first run. A truncation drops the terms it does not keep: the total indices hold only the interactions of the basis, and `loo_error` says how much of the model the smaller basis misses.

```python
additive = analysis.run(
    PolynomialChaos(degree=4, max_interaction=1, draws=30, quantities=[peak])
)
print(len(additive.indices), round(additive.loo_error[0], 4))  # 9 0.0071
print([round(s, 2) for s in additive.total[0]])  # [0.61, 0.39]
```

With one input per term, the 9 terms against the 15 of the total degree hold no interaction, so each total index equals the first-order one. Here the leave-one-out error stays small: the interaction of `k1` and `k2` adds little to the peak.

## Plots

Each result draws its own figure with `plot()`, one panel per quantity, and returns the matplotlib `Figure` ([Plotting](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#plotting): the extra `commol[plot]`, `output_file`, `config` and `axes`). The `plot` of a `PRCCResult` draws one line per input over the positions of a `Trajectory` and one bar per input for any other quantity. The `plot` of a `MorrisResult` draws `sigma` against `mu_star`, one point per input. The `plot` of a `SobolResult` draws the first-order and total indices with their intervals, and the `plot` of a `ChaosResult` draws those of the expansion.

```python
figure = over_axis.plot(x_label="Step")
figure = screening.plot()
figure = indices.plot()
```

## Checklist

- [ ] Each input has bounds and a distribution you can defend; a uniform needs finite bounds.
- [ ] Morris, Sobol and the polynomial chaos run on independent inputs; a posterior goes to PRCC or propagation.
- [ ] A stochastic engine has `replicates` and a `seed`.
- [ ] Each quantity reads the series you mean: the level of an output that only grows peaks at the last position, its `Increments` at the largest gain of a window.
- [ ] A quantity that is NaN is filtered with `where(mask)` only on a condition you can defend, and the summary is read as conditioned on it.
- [ ] The intervals of Sobol are narrow enough to rank the inputs, and none is NaN (a bootstrap replicate of no variance); if not, raise `draws`.
- [ ] The leave-one-out error of a polynomial chaos is small before you read its indices, and `predict` reads values inside the bounds of the inputs.
- [ ] A truncated basis of a polynomial chaos (`max_interaction`, `q_norm`) keeps the interactions you expect to matter; its total indices hold no other.

# Reports

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

A report turns the data of an object into plain dictionaries, ready for JSON. Each report is a method of the object whose data it describes:

| Method                                                    | Reports                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Model.applied_parameters(values, problem=None, …)`       | What the model holds and what calibration set                                                                                                        |
| `SimulationResults.report(positions, window, windows, …)` | What a run produced, next to the observations                                                                                                        |
| `SimulationReplicates.report(confidence_level, …)`        | The same, with each number reduced across the replicates of a stochastic engine                                                                      |
| `Predictive.report(confidence_level, …)`                  | The same, with each number reduced across the draws of a sample, with their weights                                                                  |
| `IdentifiabilityReport.report()`                          | The verdicts of an identifiability analysis ([Identifiability](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/identifiability/#the-report)) |

A single run and an ensemble give the same layout.

## Quick path

```python
import json

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Reported")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
        .add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
        .add_transition(
            id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total", accumulators=["cum_ab"]
        )
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            ),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )

ends = [7, 14, 21, 28]
truth = Simulation(model(0.4)).run(num_steps=28)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=end, output="cum_ab", value=count, window=7)
    for end, count in zip(ends, truth.windowed_totals(["cum_ab"], 7, ends))
]
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
)

calibrated = model(None)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(calibrated), problem).run()
calibrated.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)

applied = calibrated.applied_parameters(result, problem)
print(json.dumps(applied["parameters"]["k2"]))  # {"value": 0.1, "calibrated": false}

results = Simulation(calibrated).run(num_steps=28)
run_report = results.report(
    positions=ends,
    window=7,
    windows=4,
    observed_data=observed_data,
    accumulators=["cum_ab"],
)
print(sorted(run_report))  # ['accumulators', 'observed', 'series']
```

## The applied parameters of a model

`Model.applied_parameters(values, problem=None, sample=None, confidence_level=None)` lists every number the calibrated model holds, and whether calibration set it. The `parameters` section is the same for every kind of model; the structure of the model adds the sections of its kind (`ModelStructure.report_sections`). An aggregate model adds `initial_amounts` and `category_splits`:

```json
{
  "parameters": {
    "k1": {"value": 0.4, "calibrated": true},
    "k2": {"value": 0.1, "calibrated": false}
  },
  "initial_amounts": {
    "A": {"amount": 990.0, "unit": "item", "calibrated": false},
    "B": {"amount": 10.0, "unit": "item", "calibrated": true},
    "C": {"amount": 100000.0, "unit": "mg/l", "calibrated": false}
  },
  "category_splits": {
    "g1": {"group": [], "fraction": 0.5, "calibrated": false},
    "g2": {"group": [], "fraction": 0.5, "calibrated": false}
  }
}
```

| Argument                     | Meaning                                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The model                    | Call the method on the model **after** `apply_calibration_parameters`.                                                                  |
| `values`                     | A `CalibrationResult`, or an `{id: value}` mapping such as one of `sample.draws()`.                                                     |
| `problem`                    | Optional. Adds the calibrated `factor` and `noise` parameters, which the model does not hold.                                           |
| `sample`, `confidence_level` | Optional. A `ParameterSample`: each entry gains its weighted statistics (`ParameterSample.summary`). A sample needs a confidence level. |

| Entry                                            | Rule                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Parameters                                       | Only numeric parameters: formulas and series are inputs, not fitted values.                                                                                                                               |
| `initial_amounts`                                | One row per bin and per overridden compartment: the `amount` the engine builds, overrides included, and the `unit` of its bin. No row is a share of a total, so bins of different units sit side by side. |
| `category_splits`                                | One row per category: its `fraction` of the group it splits. A category has no amount, because it can split bins of different units.                                                                      |
| `group`                                          | The conditioning categories of a conditional stratification, or `[]` when it splits every bin.                                                                                                            |
| An uncalibrated bin (`None` amount)              | `amount` is `null`.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| A bin with no unit                               | `unit` is `null`.                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| A category name that two stratifications declare | Its row is under the qualified id, such as `group:g1`.                                                                                                                                                    |
| A `sample`                                       | Each entry gains an `interval` block (`mean`, `median`, `ci_lower`, `ci_upper`, `min`, `max`, `std`, all weighted), and the report starts with `confidence_level`.                                        |

The key order of each entry is fixed (`value`, `calibrated`, then `interval`; `amount`, `unit`, `calibrated`, then `interval`; `group`, `fraction`, `calibrated`, then `interval`), so saved JSON files stay comparable. An interval is in the unit of its entry: an amount in the unit of its bin, a split as a fraction of its group.

## The report of a run

`SimulationResults.report(positions, window, windows, observed_data=(), accumulators=(), prediction_intervals=None)` reports a run on one axis of windows. It reads each value at a position of the results (`results.positions`), so it works for any model type: a differential model reports at non-integer positions once the results hold them ([Reporting at any position](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/simulations/#reporting-at-any-position)).

| Block          | Content                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `observed`     | For each observation label: `values`, padded to `windows`, so it lines up with `windowed` index for index. An observation goes to the window that holds its position (the rule of `AxisUnits.window_index`). `outputs` and `factor_id` appear when a series uses them, `weights` when a weight is not 1.0, and `scales` when a scale is not 1.0. |
| `series`       | Each output sampled at `positions`, sorted by name, except the outputs of the accumulators in `accumulators`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `accumulators` | For each accumulator: `total` (its final value), `windowed` (the gain in each window that ends within the results, as the loss compares it) and `cumulative` (sampled at `positions`); each reading as a `total` and `by_output`                                                                                                                 |

| Argument               | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `positions`            | The positions where series and cumulative readings are sampled; each must be a position of the results (`ValueError` otherwise).                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `window`, `windows`    | The window axis of `observed` and `windowed`: the length of one window and how many.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `observed_data`        | The observations to report next to the run.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `accumulators`         | The accumulator ids to report. The results read the outputs of each one from their model (`results.model`, which `Simulation.run`, `run_at` and `replicates` set); results built by hand have no model, and reporting an accumulator raises `ValueError` that names it.                                                       |
| `prediction_intervals` | The `PredictionIntervals` of a [conformal method](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/conformal/index.md) (`ConformalResult.intervals`). The report gains a last block, `prediction_intervals`: its `confidence_level`, `series` (by label: `positions`, `prediction`, `lower`, `upper`) and `unbounded`. |

The report holds only these blocks, and `prediction_intervals` when it is given. Add your own envelope around them, such as a run label or summary figures in your domain's terms:

```python
document = {"kind": "calibration", "at": ends, **run_report}
print(json.dumps(document)[:30])
```

The results hold a reference to their model, not a copy, and a report reads only its structure (the outputs of each bin and accumulator), never the values of its parameters, so a later `update_parameters` does not change the report of a run. Results with their model still pickle.

## The report of an ensemble

`SimulationReplicates.report(confidence_level, positions, window, windows, observed_data=(), accumulators=(), prediction_intervals=None)` reports the replicates of a stochastic engine, and `Predictive.report` with the same arguments reports the draws of a [`Predictive`](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/uncertainty/#the-predictive). The layout is the one of the report of a run; every number becomes a `{mean, median, ci_lower, ci_upper, min, max}` block, computed per member and then reduced across the members with their weights (equal for replicates). A predictive takes no point estimate: each number comes from the draws only.

```python
from commol.uncertainty import ParameterSample, Predictive, SampleMethod

sample = ParameterSample.equally_weighted(
    ["k1"], [(0.0, 1.0)], [[0.35], [0.4], [0.45]], SampleMethod(name="draws")
)
predictive = Predictive(Calibrator(Simulation(model(None)), problem), sample, range(29))
band_report = predictive.report(
    0.9, positions=ends, window=7, windows=4, accumulators=["cum_ab"]
)
print(list(band_report["series"]["A"]))  # ['mean', 'median', 'ci_lower', 'ci_upper', 'min', 'max']
```

## The report of an identifiability analysis

`IdentifiabilityReport.report()` gives the result of `Calibrator.identifiability` (also with `ProfileIdentifiability`), or of `IdentifiabilityReport.merge`, as `parameters` (each parameter, in problem order, with its `structural` and `practical` verdicts, their reasons and combinations, or `None`) and `sections` (the evidence of each method that ran, by section name).

## Checklist

- [ ] The model reports `applied_parameters` after `apply_calibration_parameters`.
- [ ] `problem` is passed when there are `factor` or `noise` parameters.
- [ ] `positions`, `window` and `windows` match the observations, and the results hold every position the report reads.

# Threads and Parallelism

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

commol runs its independent work in parallel in Rust: the starts of a calibration, the replicates of a bootstrap, the particles of a swarm, the draws of a predictive. This page is for a user who wants to choose how many threads that work uses, and which levels of it run in parallel. By default, commol uses one thread per core and every level in parallel; a seed gives the same result whatever you choose.

## Quick path

```python
import commol.parallelism

commol.parallelism.set_threads(4)  # every parallel method from here on, in this thread

with commol.parallelism.threads(2):  # only inside the block
    print(commol.parallelism.get_threads(), commol.parallelism.get_levels())  # 2 all

with commol.parallelism.threads(levels="outer"):  # the particles of a swarm in order
    print(commol.parallelism.get_threads(), commol.parallelism.get_levels())  # 4 outer
```

| Name                                              | What it does                                                                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `commol.parallelism.set_threads(n, levels=None)`  | Sets the number of threads, at least 1, and optionally the levels, until the next call.                                                           |
| `commol.parallelism.threads(n=None, levels=None)` | A context manager: the setting holds inside the block and the previous one comes back after it, also on an error. `None` keeps the current value. |
| `commol.parallelism.get_threads()`                | The number of threads: the one set, or the number of cores.                                                                                       |
| `commol.parallelism.get_levels()`                 | `"all"` or `"outer"`: the levels set, or `"all"`.                                                                                                 |

A number below 1, or `levels` other than `"all"` and `"outer"`, raises `ValueError`.

## What runs in parallel

| Method                                                          | What runs in parallel                          |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| `Calibrator.run(starts=n)`                                      | The starts                                     |
| A particle swarm (`ParticleSwarmConfig`)                        | The particles of an iteration                  |
| The bootstraps, the block jackknife                             | The replicates                                 |
| `Predictive`, `Scenarios`, scores                               | The draws of the sample                        |
| `GibbsPosterior`, `BayesianPosterior`, `ABCSMC`, `ABCRejection` | The particles or the draws                     |
| `ProfileLikelihood`, `PredictionProfile`                        | Each side of each quantity                     |
| The conformal methods                                           | The fits of their folds or blocks              |
| The sensitivity methods                                         | The runs of the design                         |
| The local approximations, the identifiability methods           | The runs of the finite differences, the points |
| `Simulation.replicates(count)`                                  | The replicates of a stochastic engine          |

One run of a model is never split: each thread runs whole runs.

## The number of threads

Every parallel method runs in a pool of `n` threads that commol builds from the setting, and uses at most those threads, nested levels included. The setting is a `contextvars` variable: it holds in the Python thread, or the `asyncio` task, that sets it, and another thread starts with the default.

`commol.parallelism.threads` limits one block, for example when another library shares the machine:

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParticleSwarmConfig,
    Simulation,
)
from commol.resampling import BayesianBootstrap

def model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Threads")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_transition(id="ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A")
        .build(Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}), engine="DifferenceEquations")
    )

run = Simulation(model(0.2)).run(20)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=t, output="B", value=run["B"][t]) for t in range(2, 21, 2)
    ],
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=ParticleSwarmConfig(particles=10, max_iterations=30),
    seed=3,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(model(None)), problem)

with commol.parallelism.threads(2):
    fit = calibrator.run(starts=4)
    bootstrap = calibrator.uncertainty(BayesianBootstrap(replicates=8, block_length=1))
print(round(fit.best_parameters["k1"], 3))  # 0.2
```

## The levels

Some methods nest one parallel level in another: the starts of a calibration each run a swarm, and so do the replicates of a bootstrap. `levels` chooses which of them run in parallel:

| `levels`          | The outer level (starts, replicates, draws) | The particles of a swarm |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `"all"` (default) | In parallel                                 | In parallel              |
| `"outer"`         | In parallel                                 | One after the other      |

With `"all"`, both levels share the one pool, and a thread with no work takes work from another one, so a calibration with one start uses every thread and a run with fewer starts than threads fills the gaps. `"outer"` keeps the particles of a swarm in order.

The levels change no result: a seed gives the same result with any number of threads and either level, bit for bit, the history of `Calibrator.run_with_history` included.

```python
with commol.parallelism.threads(4, levels="outer"):
    in_order = calibrator.run_with_history()
with commol.parallelism.threads(4, levels="all"):
    in_parallel = calibrator.run_with_history()
print(in_order == in_parallel)  # True
```

## `RAYON_NUM_THREADS`

commol does not read the environment variable `RAYON_NUM_THREADS` of the `rayon` library, and does not use the global thread pool of `rayon`. Use `commol.parallelism.set_threads` instead. Another library of the process that uses `rayon` keeps its own setting.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                         | Try                                                                            |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| commol takes every core from other work         | `commol.parallelism.set_threads(n)` with fewer threads                         |
| A setting does not hold in a thread you started | Set it in that thread: each Python thread has its own                          |
| A calibration with one start uses one core      | Check `commol.parallelism.get_levels()`: `"outer"` runs the particles in order |

## Example 1: A chain of states

`A` moves to `B` at an absolute rate, which names compartments, and `B` moves to `C` at a proportional rate, which names none. A fourth state `M` sits between `A` and `B`:

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Chain Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="M", name="Intermediate")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.4, description="A to M rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.2, description="M to B rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k3", value=0.1, description="B to C rate")
    .add_transition(id="flow_AM", source=["A"], target=["M"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_MB", source=["M"], target=["B"], rate="k2")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k3")
    .build(
        Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 999, "M": 0, "B": 1, "C": 0}),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)

peak = max(results["B"])
print(f"B peaks at {peak:.0f} at step {results['B'].index(peak)}")
results.plot.series(output_file="chain.png")
```

## Example 2: A periodic rate

The rate of `A` to `B` varies with a period of 365 steps; `step` is the position on the axis and `pi` a constant of the [expressions](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/guide/mathematical-expressions/index.md):

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Periodic Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k_mean", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k_amp", value=0.2)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="periodic_flow",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k_mean * (1 + k_amp * sin(2 * pi * step / 365)) * A * B / total",
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=365 * 3)
results.plot.series(series=["B"], tick_every=365, output_file="periodic.png")
```

## Example 3: A rate per group

A stratification splits every bin into three groups, and the transition from `B` to `C` has one rate per group. In a figure, a bin id such as `B` draws the sum of its compartments:

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    ModelBuilder,
    Simulation,
    StratificationCondition,
    StratifiedRate,
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stratified Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2", "g3"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.0003)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g1", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g2", value=0.12)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g3", value=0.08)
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        stratified_rates=[
            StratifiedRate(
                conditions=[
                    StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="g1")
                ],
                rate="k2_g1",
            ),
            StratifiedRate(
                conditions=[
                    StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="g2")
                ],
                rate="k2_g2",
            ),
            StratifiedRate(
                conditions=[
                    StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="g3")
                ],
                rate="k2_g3",
            ),
        ],
    )
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9900, "B": 100, "C": 0},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.25, "g2": 0.55, "g3": 0.2}},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)

for name in ["B_g1", "B_g2", "B_g3"]:
    print(f"{name}: {results[name][-1]:.2f}")
results.plot.series(series=["B", "B_g1", "B_g3"], output_file="groups.png")
```

## Example 4: Rates of an intersection

Two stratifications, and a rate for the compartments of type `t2` only. In group `g1`, the rate divides by the total of the subgroup, `total_g1`, instead of the total of the model. `per_compartment=True` makes `A` and `B` in the rate the compartments of each flow, so each compartment of `A` loses an amount computed from its own amount:

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    ModelBuilder,
    Simulation,
    StratificationCondition,
    StratifiedRate,
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Intersection Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(id="type", categories=["t1", "t2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1_low", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k1_high", value=0.6)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1_low * A * B / total",
        stratified_rates=[
            StratifiedRate(
                conditions=[
                    StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="g1")
                ],
                rate="k1_low * A * B / total_g1",
            ),
            StratifiedRate(
                conditions=[
                    StratificationCondition(stratification="type", category="t2")
                ],
                rate="k1_high * A * B / total",
            ),
        ],
        per_compartment=True,
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            stratification_fractions={
                "group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4},
                "type": {"t1": 0.8, "t2": 0.2},
            },
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)
print(sorted(name for name in results if name.startswith("B_")))
# ['B_g1_t1', 'B_g1_t2', 'B_g2_t1', 'B_g2_t2']
```

## Example 5: A conditional stratification

The stratification `subtype` splits only the compartments of group `g2`; the compartments of `g1` are not split further:

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    ModelBuilder,
    Simulation,
    StratificationCondition,
    StratifiedRate,
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Conditional Stratification Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(
        id="subtype",
        categories=["s1", "s2"],
        conditions=[StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="g2")],
    )
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_default", value=0.1)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_s1", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_s2", value=0.05)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1 * A * B / total",
        per_compartment=True,
    )
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2_default",
        stratified_rates=[
            StratifiedRate(
                conditions=[
                    StratificationCondition(stratification="subtype", category="s1")
                ],
                rate="k2_s1",
            ),
            StratifiedRate(
                conditions=[
                    StratificationCondition(stratification="subtype", category="s2")
                ],
                rate="k2_s2",
            ),
        ],
    )
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9900, "B": 100, "C": 0},
            stratification_fractions={
                "group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4},
                "subtype": {"s1": 0.7, "s2": 0.3},
            },
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)
print(sorted(name for name in results if name.startswith("B")))
# ['B_g1', 'B_g2_s1', 'B_g2_s2']
```

## Example 6: A capacity limit

The flow from `B` slows as `C` fills, and stops when `C` reaches `capacity`. The rate names `B`, so it is the flow itself; the factor `max(0, 1 - C / capacity)` never turns it negative. A difference model moves the flow of a whole step at once, so the last step can pass `capacity` by a little:

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Capacity Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.5)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_max", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="capacity", value=100.0)
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2_max * B * max(0, 1 - C / capacity)",
    )
    .build(
        Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 950, "B": 50, "C": 0}),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)
print(round(results["C"][-1], 1))  # 100.0
```

## Example 7: A cycle in continuous time

Amounts in `C` return to `A`, so the process never ends. The same process runs as differential equations: only the engine changes, and the results can be read at any position, here every half step:

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Cyclic Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_parameter(id="k3", value=0.01, description="C to A rate")
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .add_transition(id="return_CA", source=["C"], target=["A"], rate="k3")
    .build(
        Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
        engine="DifferentialEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run_at([step / 2 for step in range(2001)])
print(results.positions[:3])  # [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]
print(round(sum(results[name][-1] for name in ["A", "B", "C"])))  # 1000
```

## Example 8: Rates that follow a pattern

An `AxisPattern` is a rate that changes along the axis. The first model combines an opening pulse, an event every 30 steps and a sinusoid. The second gives each group its own schedule: the first `add_group` call is on the class, the next ones on the pattern it returns:

```python
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    AxisPattern,
    ModelBuilder,
    Simulation,
    StratificationCondition,
)

combined = AxisPattern.combine(
    AxisPattern.pulse(at=0, value=0.3),
    AxisPattern.periodic(period=30, value=0.05),
    AxisPattern.sinusoid(amplitude=0.005, period=365, baseline=0.01),
)
model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Pattern Model")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="Source")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="Sink")
    .add_transition(id="flow", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate=combined)
    .build(Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 10000, "B": 0}), engine="DifferenceEquations")
)
results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=365)

per_group = AxisPattern.add_group(
    conditions=[StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="cat1")],
    schedule=AxisPattern.periodic(period=7, value=0.05),
).add_group(
    conditions=[StratificationCondition(stratification="group", category="cat2")],
    schedule=AxisPattern.periodic(period=30, value=0.05),
)
grouped = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Schedule Model")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="Source")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="Sink")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["cat1", "cat2"])
    .add_transition(id="flow", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate=per_group)
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"cat1": 0.5, "cat2": 0.5}},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)
grouped_results = Simulation(grouped).run(num_steps=60)
print(grouped_results["B_cat1"][-1] > grouped_results["B_cat2"][-1])  # True
```

## Example 9: Runs at random

The `StochasticSteps` engine moves whole units at random, one step at a time. `replicates` runs the model once per seed; the mean, the band and the figure reduce the runs position by position:

```python
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stochastic Model")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}), engine="StochasticSteps")
)

replicates = Simulation(model).replicates(40, seed=7).run(num_steps=100)
mean = replicates.mean()
spread = replicates.member_statistics("C", confidence_level=0.9)
print(round(mean["C"][-1]), round(spread["ci_lower"][-1]), round(spread["ci_upper"][-1]))
replicates.plot.series(series=["B", "C"], confidence_level=0.9, output_file="replicates.png")
```

## Example 10: A fit, its uncertainty and two scenarios

A fit of `k1` to noisy observations of `B`, a sample of `k1` from a Bayesian bootstrap, its predictive band, and a comparison of two scenarios of `k2`. The work of the bootstrap and of the draws runs on two threads:

```python
import numpy as np

import commol.parallelism
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)
from commol.resampling import BayesianBootstrap
from commol.uncertainty import Predictive, Scenarios
from commol.quantities import ValueAt
from commol.plotting import plot_compared


def basic_model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4)).run(num_steps=40)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step] * float(np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.05))))
    for step in range(2, 41, 2)
]
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(basic_model(None)), problem)

with commol.parallelism.threads(2):
    fit = calibrator.run()
    bootstrap = calibrator.uncertainty(BayesianBootstrap(replicates=20, block_length=1))
    predictive = Predictive(calibrator, bootstrap.sample, positions=list(range(61)))
    scenarios = Scenarios(
        calibrator,
        bootstrap.sample,
        {"fitted": {}, "slower": {"k2": 0.05}},
        positions=list(range(61)),
    )

print(round(fit.best_parameters["k1"], 2))  # close to 0.4
lower, upper = bootstrap.sample.interval(0.9)["k1"]
print(round(lower, 3), round(upper, 3))  # the 90 % interval of k1
predictive.plot.series(series=["B"], observed_data=observed_data, output_file="band.png")

[difference] = scenarios.compare("slower", "fitted", [ValueAt(series="C", at=60)], 0.9)
print(difference.label, round(difference.median))  # how much less C reaches by step 60
plot_compared(scenarios, series=["B", "C"], output_file="scenarios.png")
```

# API reference

# API Reference

[Back to Home](https://munqu.github.io/commol/latest/index.md)

Every public name of `commol`, generated from the docstrings. The guide pages explain how to use them; these pages list every argument, attribute and error.

The package root `commol` holds the main flow: build a model, choose its structure, simulate it and calibrate it, as in `from commol import Simulation`. Every other name lives in the module of its page of the guide, as in `from commol.resampling import BayesianBootstrap`; each module has its page here. A name you only read is not exported: a result is typed as the return of the member that gives it, and it is on the page of that object, as `SimulationResults` is on the Simulation page. A choice among names is a string, such as `loss_function="sse"`.
